eras.name: Laboratory & coin-op
eras.essay: Four mechanics in this window, and two of them are load-bearing for everything else. Spacewar! contributes Object Collision As Verb in 1962 — two things occupy the same space and something happens — which is the direct ancestor of hit points, combos, ragdolls, destructible walls, and line-of-sight detection. Pong then contributes three at once in 1972: Single-Screen Arena, where the frame is the entire world; Numeric Score, the first thing a game ever remembered about a player; and Same-Screen Two-Player, which remains the most legible multiplayer arrangement anyone has built. Notice what is absent. No persistence beyond the session, no fiction, no camera worth naming, no economy other than the coin. Games in this period are being defined by what the hardware can hold rather than by what anyone wants to say, and the mechanics that survive are the ones cheap enough to compute in real time. Gun Fight, Breakout, Night Driver, and Combat all appear here as adopters rather than originators, refining collision into recognizable forms.

eras.name: The home cartridge
eras.essay: Twenty-six mechanics originate in these eight years, the densest concentration in the dataset relative to the number of games shipping. Space Invaders introduces Lives and Continues alongside the Coin-Op Difficulty Economy, which is the first time monetization directly authored a difficulty curve. Asteroids adds Wraparound Topology and the Persistent High-Score Table. Defender decouples the camera from the playfield with the Continuous Scrolling Playfield, arguably the most consequential spatial idea before 3D, while Battlezone puts the camera inside the world at eye level and Adventure turns the world into a graph of rooms. Rogue alone accounts for five entries in 1980: procedural levels, experience points, permadeath, hit points, and the food clock. Everything the arcade cannot do, the home computer does — Wizardry adds Character Classes, Castle Wolfenstein gives enemies the capacity to fail to see you, Lode Runner ships a level editor in the box, Ultima III starts a clock the player does not control, and Elite computes eight galaxies from a seed. Fiction arrives late and sideways, through Pac-Man's interludes and Dragon's Lair's timed prompts.

eras.name: 8- and 16-bit
eras.essay: Consoles get memory, and memory changes what a game can be about. Metroid's Password Continuation and The Legend of Zelda's Battery-Backed Save File let a game be longer than one sitting, which is what invents the campaign; Metroid's Ability-Gated Interlocked Map makes progression spatial rather than linear. Super Mario Bros. teaches players a physical vocabulary through Momentum-Based Platform Control instead of a binary one. Ultima IV proposes Branching Dialogue Trees and an Explicit Morality Axis in the same release, and Ultima VII gives its characters daily schedules. Street Fighter II's Chained Combo Strings begin as a bug and become a skill ceiling nobody designed. Dune II lands two roots at once — Real-Time Base and Unit Production and Fog of War — neither with a parent in this data. Doom closes the period with four separate entries: Networked Deathmatch, In-Game Automap, Selectable Difficulty, and Open Data Formats and Mod SDK, the last of which turns players into an unpaid apprenticeship pipeline whose graduates ship Counter-Strike and Defense of the Ancients.

eras.name: The 3D rupture
eras.essay: Forty-one mechanics originate here, more than any other period, because 3D invalidated solved problems and forced the medium to re-answer them. Quake supplies true polygonal space and the authoritative client-server model in one release. Super Mario 64 supplies four, among them Analog Free-Roam 3D Movement, Trailing Follow Camera, and Graded Analog Input, and creates the camera problem that Resident Evil answers with fixed angles and Ocarina of Time answers with lock-on targeting. Diablo contributes four, including Branching Skill Tree and Colour-Coded Loot Rarity, and Ultima Online contributes the Persistent Shared World with an economy and a society inside it. 1998 is remarkable on its own: Metal Gear Solid's Graduated Alert States and Explicit Detection Feedback, Thief's Light-and-Shadow Stealth and Diegetic 3D Audio Information, Rainbow Six's iron sights, Baldur's Gate's quest journal, and Trespasser's ragdolls. System Shock had already solved storytelling without cutscenes through Environmental Storytelling and the Found Audio Log, an answer the industry is still using.

eras.name: Broadband & the console shooter
eras.essay: Thirty-seven mechanics, and an unusual number of them are still the default today. Halo: Combat Evolved ships Regenerating Health, Constrained Weapon Loadout, the Persistent Minimap / Radar, and Drop-In Co-op Campaign in one 2001 release; Halo 2 follows with Automated Skill Matchmaking, which deletes the server browser and makes ranked play a console-scale product. Grand Theft Auto III makes the city contiguous with Seamless Streaming Open World and then makes it navigable with the Waypoint Objective Marker. kill.switch introduces Over-the-Shoulder Aim and Snap-to-Cover Combat two years before Resident Evil 4 and Gears of War canonize them. Call of Duty 4 fuses the two lineages with Perk-Based Loadout Customization, Prestige Reset-for-Status, and Persistent Multiplayer Progression, where losing still pays. Elsewhere: Half-Life 2 makes physics a puzzle vocabulary, Nintendogs and Wii Sports remove the intermediary between hand and game, MapleStory imports free-to-play, and BioShock makes the player's compliance the subject of the story.

eras.name: Digital storefronts & indie
eras.essay: Distribution changes who can originate a mechanic, and the origins in this period reflect it. Minecraft accounts for four entries — Editable Voxel Terrain, Free-Form Base Building, Infinite Chunked World, and Paid Early Access Development — from a team that started at one person. Rogue Legacy's Run-Persistent Meta-Progression is the compromise that made roguelikes mass-market by letting the player keep something after losing the run. BeamNG.drive spends everything on Soft-Body Deformation. Meanwhile the largest studios are re-engineering the business model in public: Team Fortress 2's Randomized Loot Box, League of Legends' Cosmetic-Only Monetization, L.A. Noire's Season Pass Bundle, Candy Crush Saga's mobile free-to-play, Dota 2's Seasonal Battle Pass, and Destiny's Live-Service Seasonal Content, which turns the game into a calendar. FromSoftware's contributions bracket the period — Demon's Souls with Stamina Action Economy and Poise and Stagger Break, Dark Souls with Bonfire Checkpoint & Currency Risk — and Left 4 Dead's Dynamic AI Director makes pacing itself a system.

eras.name: Live service & the long tail
eras.essay: Fourteen mechanics originate in this window, and the newest entry in the entire dataset is from 2020, which is a claim about evidence rather than about the industry. Recent origins are synthetic in the precise sense: Breath of the Wild fuses Systemic Climbable Surfaces with Stamina Action Economy to produce Climb-Anything Stamina Traversal, and fuses Far Cry 2's propagating fire with Half-Life 2's rigid bodies to produce Systemic Elemental Chemistry. PUBG combines matchmaking with Rogue's food clock and gets the Shrinking-Circle Battle Royale; Escape from Tarkov adds permadeath to that and gets extraction. Slay the Spire merges a card game with a roguelike run. Sekiro resolves a twenty-year argument between parrying and stamina. Elsewhere, Apex Legends' Non-Verbal Ping Communication and The Last of Us Part II's Comprehensive Accessibility Suite treat access as a design surface, Fortnite drops platform walls, and Half-Life: Alyx restates the camera problem by making it the player's neck.

f_collision.name: Object Collision As Verb
f_collision.summary: Object collision is the rule that two things touching in a game's coordinate space causes an event, the primitive underneath every hit, landing, block and death in the medium.
prose: At its simplest, collision detection asks whether two shapes overlap this frame, and collision response decides what that overlap means. A pair of coordinates and radii is enough: if the distance between torpedo and ship falls below a threshold, the ship is destroyed. Everything expressive about it lives in the response half. Same test, different verb, and you have a bullet, a footstep on solid ground, a locked door, or a catch.

Spacewar! arrived in 1962 on a PDP-1 at MIT, where Steve Russell and his collaborators had a vector display, scarce memory, and no precedent to copy. Two ships, two torpedoes, and a star: for any of it to be a game rather than an animation, the program had to notice contact and act on it. Hardware offered no help, so the test was arithmetic, run every frame on positions the program already tracked.

Because contact is cheap to compute and endlessly reinterpretable, it became the substrate rather than a feature. Genres separate mostly by what they do after the overlap: subtract hit points, stop movement, start a grab animation, deform a mesh. Costs followed. Collision is where cheating, lag compensation and hitbox arguments live, and a mismatch between the visible body and the tested shape is still one of the most common sources of felt unfairness.

f_score.name: Numeric Score
f_score.summary: A numeric score is a running total the game keeps on the player's behalf, the earliest form of memory in the medium and the ancestor of every progression system that followed.
prose: Events are assigned point values, points accumulate, and the total is displayed. Nothing else is required: no save file, no identity, no persistence between sessions. Because that number is the only feedback which survives a moment of play, it becomes the yardstick for everything, which means a designer's choice of what to reward is effectively a statement about what the game is for.

Pong displayed two digits in 1972 because it had to, since a competitive game needs a way to declare a winner and Atari's hardware could count. Arcade economics then made scores central, because a machine has to tell strangers who did well and why they should try again. Scoring also solved a design problem for games with no ending, giving open-ended activity a way to say the player improved.

Points shaped decades of play and then quietly retreated. Once games gained saves, stories and progression, an abstract number stopped explaining what a player had achieved, and score now survives mainly where mastery is the explicit subject. Its logic did not vanish, though. Experience, gear level, ranks and achievements are all scores with better dressing, and the same critique applies to all of them: the metric distorts the play.

f_hotseat.name: Same-Screen Two-Player
f_hotseat.summary: Same-screen two-player puts two people at one display with their own controls, so both see identical information and every action is immediately visible to the person sitting beside you.
prose: One screen, two inputs, no hidden state. Both players share a camera, which constrains design absolutely: action has to fit a single view, so arenas are bounded, movement is coupled, and nothing can be concealed from an opponent looking at the same pixels. Social consequence arrives instantly, because winning and losing happen next to somebody whose face you can see while it is happening.

Atari released Pong in 1972 as a two-player cabinet, since a machine of that period could model a ball and two paddles but not an opponent. Precedence is genuinely contested: Magnavox's home console reached the market the same year with a similar tennis game, and university machines had run competitive two-player games through the 1960s. What Pong established commercially was the coin-operated social contest.

Local competition remains the most legible form the medium has, requiring no tutorial, no account and no explanation, and its constraints produced entire genres. Costs are physical: both people must be in the room, screens are limited in size, and a single camera forbids exploration, secrecy or scale. Online play solved those problems and lost the thing that made the format work, which is presence.

f_single_screen.name: Single-Screen Arena
f_single_screen.summary: A single-screen arena keeps the entire playable world inside one unscrolling frame, so every object on display is in play and nothing important sits off-camera waiting to be found.
prose: Everything the game contains occupies one fixed frame. There is no camera motion, no off-screen simulation, and no map larger than the display; objects that reach an edge bounce, die, or wrap. Since the player sees the whole system at once, difficulty has to come from density, speed and timing rather than from concealment. Reading the board and reading the game are the same act, which is why these designs stay legible to a stranger.

Atari's Pong in 1972 ran on discrete logic rather than a processor, with no memory to store a world and no way to redraw one. What the circuit could do was position two paddles, a ball and a score, and that budget defined the shape of the game. Coin-operated cabinets reinforced it: a passerby had to understand the whole thing from a few seconds of watching over someone's shoulder.

Confinement produced a design culture built on escalation and pattern rather than exploration or story, and it made the arcade's economics work, since a two-minute game needs no context. What it foreclosed was scale of every kind: no travel, no persistence, no place to hide information. Later games recovered the form deliberately, using the fixed frame as a way to promise the player that all the evidence is already visible.

f_coin_op.name: Coin-Op Difficulty Economy
f_coin_op.summary: Coin-op difficulty economies tune a game's challenge curve to the length of a paid session, ending most attempts within a few minutes so that continuing requires feeding the machine again.
prose: Design targets a duration rather than a completion. Difficulty rises continuously, lives are few, and the ceiling is set so an average player finishes in two or three minutes while an expert is permitted a long run that works as advertising. Operators adjust the settings physically, through switches inside the cabinet that change starting lives and bonus thresholds to suit a particular location's takings.

Taito released Space Invaders in 1978, where a hardware limitation produced the effect almost by accident: as the player destroyed aliens, the machine had fewer sprites to draw and the survivors accelerated. Pressure rose exactly as the field emptied. Whether or not that acceleration was intended, the lesson was read clearly across the industry, and deliberate tuning toward the next coin became standard arcade practice.

Monetisation authored the difficulty curve, and the habits it produced outlived the cabinet: continue timers, finite lives, and a general sense that failure carries a price. Home conversions inherited curves designed for a coin slot and often felt punitive without one. Later free-to-play economies rebuilt the same relationship with an unlimited slot, which is why arcade tuning is usually the first ancestor named when those systems are examined.

adoptedBy.name: Street Fighter II: The World Warrior

f_lives_continues.name: Lives and Continues
f_lives_continues.summary: Lives and continues turn failure into a budget: a player is given a fixed number of attempts, and running out ends the session unless more can be bought or earned.
prose: Player begins with a small stock of lives; each death spends one and returns them to a start point with the world partly reset. Exhausting the stock ends the game, at which point a continue may allow resumption, often with penalties or from an earlier position. Structure quietly defines a session's length and shape, since the real unit of play is not the level but the stock of remaining attempts.

Taito's Space Invaders in 1978 needed the arcade to work as a business, which means each session has to end and the ending has to feel like the player's own fault. Lives did both while softening a single mistake. Continues arrived as an explicit price on failure, which is where the tension in arcade design lives, because the knob that sets challenge also sets revenue per cabinet.

Consequences outlived the coin box. Home ports inherited a difficulty curve tuned to extract money, and games spent years unlearning it, replacing lives with checkpoints and eventually removing the counter altogether. Where it survives it is usually deliberate, as scarcity that gives a run stakes. Free-to-play then rediscovered the mechanism exactly, with an energy meter in place of lives and a purchase in place of a coin.

adoptedBy.name: Commander Keen in Invasion of the Vorticons

f_high_score_table.name: Persistent High-Score Table
f_high_score_table.summary: A persistent high-score table stores the best results and the initials of whoever set them, creating the first player identity to outlive a session and the first leaderboard.
prose: Top results are held in battery-backed memory alongside a short string entered by the player, usually three letters chosen with a joystick. Table survives power cycles, so a machine accumulates a local history. Effect is social rather than mechanical, because the game becomes a standing record of the people who have played it, and beating a number becomes a way of addressing a specific stranger.

Atari's Asteroids in 1979 popularised entering initials after a good run, and the practice spread across the arcade almost immediately. Attribution is contested in detail, since earlier cabinets recorded initials too, but Asteroids is the game that made the ritual standard. Motivation was competitive and commercial at once, as a leaderboard gives a regular player something to defend and a reason to return to one particular machine.

Persistence of a name changed play from a private activity into a public claim, and it is the direct ancestor of online leaderboards, ranked ladders, achievements and profile pages. Costs appeared with the audience. Scores invite optimisation until the intended game is hollowed out, they reward time available as much as skill, and once tables went online they attracted cheating serious enough to require verification communities.

f_screen_wrap.name: Wraparound Topology
f_screen_wrap.summary: Wraparound topology joins opposite edges of the playfield so that leaving one side returns you at the other, turning a flat rectangle into a looping surface with no walls.
prose: Coordinates are taken modulo the width and height of the field, so the right edge is the left edge and the top is the bottom. Nothing is lost by travelling; there is no corner to be trapped in and no boundary to bounce off. Objects have to be drawn twice while straddling a seam, and pursuit becomes strange, because any chase can be resolved by running the wrong way for long enough.

Asteroids, released by Atari in 1979, is where the idea became legible to players. Wrapping solved a specific problem for a game about drifting momentum: a ship with no brakes will otherwise pile into a wall, and rocks that leave the screen have to go somewhere. Modular arithmetic was cheaper than either fencing the field or spawning replacements, and it kept every fragment of every asteroid permanently in play.

Consequences run in two directions. As a play space, wrapping removes the safety of corners and forces continuous attention in every direction, which is why it suits games about drift and crowd control. As an idea, it established that a game's space needs no physical analogue and can be defined by whatever rule the program applies to a coordinate, an argument that later games would push considerably further.

f_attract_premise.name: Attract-Mode Premise
f_attract_premise.summary: Attract-mode premise uses short non-interactive vignettes between rounds to establish character and situation, the first fiction to reach arcade players with no gameplay attached to it.
prose: Vignettes play automatically between stages, or while a cabinet waits for a coin. Nothing is controllable; characters simply act out a relationship, usually in a few seconds and using the same sprites the game already contains. Cost is close to zero and the payoff is characterisation, since a pursuer that is briefly pursued becomes a personality rather than a hazard. Attract sequences also demonstrated play to passers-by.

Namco's Pac-Man in 1980 inserted brief cartoons between mazes, in which a ghost chases and is then chased. Reason was partly commercial and partly humane, because a game with no ending needs punctuation, and a cabinet in a room full of competitors has to be watchable when nobody is playing. Character was also a deliberate strategy, aimed at an audience beyond the young men who played shooters.

Consequence was that fiction entered arcade games through the gaps rather than through the play, establishing a division of labour the medium has never fully resolved. Story arrived as something shown between the interactive parts, which is the direct ancestor of the cutscene and of every argument about cutscenes. Merchandising followed at once, since a character with a personality can leave the cabinet entirely.

f_side_scroll.name: Continuous Scrolling Playfield
f_side_scroll.summary: A continuous scrolling playfield lets the camera move independently of the world, so a level extends past the edges of the display and the screen becomes a window rather than a container.
prose: World data is stored larger than the display, and the visible region is a moving window over it. Hardware or software shifts the background as the player advances, streaming in new terrain at one edge while discarding it at the other. Two design questions arrive immediately: what drives the camera, and what happens to things behind the player. Answers to those questions still separate a runner from a platformer from a brawler.

Williams Electronics released Defender in 1980 with a playfield several screens wide, a scanner strip showing the parts you could not see, and a ship that flies in both directions. Credit here is not clean, because several 1980 cabinets scrolled, Namco's Rally-X among them, and tile-shifting hardware was becoming standard rather than exotic. Defender's contribution was making off-screen events matter: humans are abducted where you are not looking.

Once the world outgrew the screen, level design became a discipline of pacing and sequence rather than arrangement, and games gained the ability to withhold what lies ahead. Costs came with it. Off-screen simulation is expensive and often faked, the camera turns into a permanent design problem, and players lose the total information a fixed frame provided. Nearly every 2D genre after 1980 is a variation on this window.

adoptedBy.name: Zelda II: The Adventure of Link

f_xp_levels.name: Experience Points and Levels
f_xp_levels.summary: Experience points and levels convert repeated actions into permanent capability, giving a character a number that rises with use and thresholds that grant new power when crossed.
prose: Actions award experience, usually combat, and crossing a threshold raises a level, which improves statistics and unlocks abilities. Curve between thresholds is where the design lives, since it controls how long a player stays in each region of difficulty and how much repetition is expected. Because it accumulates, the system also supplies a reliable answer to any failure, which is to become stronger rather than to play better.

Rogue brought the idea into computer games around 1980, taking it directly from tabletop role-playing, where Dungeons & Dragons had already established levels as the currency of character growth. Translation was natural because a computer is good at exactly the bookkeeping a human table finds tedious. Early digital role-playing games adopted it wholesale, and the convention was fixed long before anyone asked whether other genres needed it.

Ubiquity is the story. Levels now appear in shooters, sports games, racing games and mobile puzzles because they reliably keep players engaged, which makes them an economic tool as much as a design one. Costs are grinding, scaled enemies that make progress feel illusory, and the way an ascending number can substitute for genuine improvement. Games that reject levels usually do so as an explicit design statement.

f_maze_fp.name: First-Person Vector Space
f_maze_fp.summary: First-person vector space places the camera at eye level inside the world and draws that world as wireframe lines, giving the player a viewpoint rather than a view of a character.
prose: Geometry is stored as line segments, transformed each frame into the viewer's frame of reference, then projected onto the screen as glowing edges. No surfaces, no textures, no lighting: distance is communicated by how the lines converge and how quickly they grow. Because drawing cost scales with the number of lines rather than with pixels, large open spaces are cheap and detail is not, which is why these worlds feel empty and vast.

Battlezone put this in arcades for Atari in 1980, with a periscope hood, a tank that turns on its treads and volcanoes on the horizon. Earlier first-person experiments exist, notably the networked 1970s program Maze War, so Battlezone is better described as the moment the viewpoint reached the public than as the moment it was invented. Vector displays made the choice practical, since they draw lines directly instead of filling a raster.

Putting the camera in the body changed what a game could ask of a player: orientation, spatial memory and judging distance in depth all become skills. It also cost the player their avatar, and with it the readability of a third-person frame, which is one reason first-person games lean so heavily on their heads-up displays. Dungeon crawlers took the viewpoint into grids and menus; shooters took it into speed.

adoptedBy.name: Ultima I: The First Age of Darkness

f_flip_screen.name: Flip-Screen Room Graph
f_flip_screen.summary: Flip-screen room graphs build a world from discrete single-screen rooms joined by exits, so moving between spaces is a hard cut rather than a camera pan across continuous ground.
prose: Each room is a self-contained screen with its own layout, contents and inhabitants. Crossing an edge swaps the whole display for the adjoining room, and the game holds only one at a time in memory. Structure therefore lives in the connections rather than in geometry: a designer authors a graph of rooms and the doors between them, and the player builds a mental map out of transitions rather than measured distance.

Atari's Adventure, written by Warren Robinett and released in 1980, adapted the text game Colossal Cave into pictures on a console with barely more than a hundred bytes of working memory. Holding a large continuous world was impossible; holding one screen and a pointer to its neighbours was not. Rooms also gave a cheap way to hide things, since a dragon or a key simply exists in a room you have not entered.

Room graphs made worlds that are large without being continuous, and they turned mapping into a player activity, first on graph paper and later through an in-game automap. Discreteness also became an aesthetic tool: a hard cut can conceal what is coming, which is why survival horror and puzzle design kept the form long after hardware could scroll. Cost is friction, since every doorway is a small interruption.

f_hitpoints.name: Hit Points
f_hitpoints.summary: Hit points express a character's remaining capacity to absorb damage as a depleting number, so a blow reduces a pool instead of instantly ending the fight or the life.
prose: Damage becomes arithmetic. Attacks subtract a value, healing adds one, zero means death, and nearly everything else in the design hangs off that single scalar: difficulty tuning, item pricing, monster placement, the pacing of a dungeon. Because the pool is just a number it can also be displayed as a bar, capped, regenerated, or grown with experience, and most combat systems since have been built by attaching further rules to it.

Michael Toy, Glenn Wichman and Ken Arnold gave Rogue hit points around 1980, inheriting them wholesale from tabletop role-playing rules that had circulated since the mid-1970s. Credit is properly shared: the idea predates the medium, and other early mainframe dungeon games used the same borrowed arithmetic. What Rogue contributed was pairing the pool with permadeath and randomly generated floors, where a shrinking number becomes a running judgement about how much further you dare go.

Quantifying survival turned combat into a negotiation rather than a coin flip, which is what made difficulty tunable at all. It also imported an odd model of injury, in which a character at one hit point fights exactly as well as one at full health, and it rewards attrition play that designers have fought ever since with stamina bars, wound states, armour layers and regeneration. Every alternative is still measured against it.

f_permadeath.name: Permadeath Run Structure
f_permadeath.summary: Permadeath means a run ends for good when the character dies, with the save file erased, so every decision carries consequences that reloading cannot undo.
prose: Save exists only to suspend a session, and it is deleted on resumption or on death. Player therefore cannot scout an outcome and retry it, which changes how information is valued: unknown items are gambles, retreat is a real option, and resources hoarded for a later floor may never be used. Difficulty is not about the hardest moment but about surviving a long chain of merely risky ones.

Rogue, written by Michael Toy, Glenn Wichman and Ken Arnold around 1980 on university Unix systems, combined it with generated dungeons because both answered the same constraint. Nobody could author enough content for repeated play, and shared machines made copying a save file both easy to detect and unsporting. Erasing progress also solved a design problem, since when a level is generated fresh, losing a run costs a situation rather than a story.

Consequence attaches emotional weight to ordinary decisions, which is why permadeath produces the anecdotes players tell each other. It also makes games hostile to interruption, punishes learning by exploration, and can turn a long run's ending into wasted time rather than drama. Most modern designs compromise, keeping the deletion but adding something that persists, which is a different mechanic with a different psychology.

f_procgen_dungeon.name: Procedurally Generated Levels
f_procgen_dungeon.summary: Procedurally generated levels build their layout at runtime from rules and a random seed, so the arrangement of rooms, monsters and items has never been played by anyone, including the designer.
prose: Rather than loading a hand-built map, a generator assembles one on demand: partition the space, place rooms, connect them with corridors, distribute enemies and items against a difficulty curve, then verify that the result can actually be finished. Verification matters as much as generation, since an unreachable staircase ruins a run. Each new game repeats the process, so player knowledge transfers as tactics rather than as memorised routes.

Michael Toy, Glenn Wichman and Ken Arnold wrote Rogue in 1980 on university machines with very little storage and a text terminal for a display. Generating a dungeon cost a few kilobytes of code where storing hundreds of them would have cost far more, and the constraint that forced the choice also made the game endlessly replayable. Similar experiments were running on other campus systems at the same time.

Content became effectively unlimited and, more usefully, unmemorisable, which is why the technique still underwrites whole genres decades later. Consistency is what it costs. A generator produces competent averages rather than authored peaks, difficulty spikes without warning, and its output can read as furniture arranged by a rulebook. Most modern implementations hand-build rooms and let the algorithm assemble them, trading pure novelty for quality control.

originDeveloper.name: Michael Toy, Glenn Wichman, Ken Arnold

f_survival_needs.name: Survival Needs Clock
f_survival_needs.summary: A survival needs clock drains hunger, thirst or warmth over time, so standing still is itself a losing move and the player is under pressure with no enemy anywhere on screen.
prose: One or more meters fall continuously. Crossing a threshold applies penalties, usually stat loss first and damage later, and restoring the meter costs a consumable that has to be found, bought, farmed or cooked. Effect on play is temporal rather than spatial: the clock forbids indefinite caution, turns exploration into a supply problem, and makes every detour a calculation about whether the return trip is affordable.

Rogue included a food clock around 1980 for a specific reason. Without one, a patient player can grind a randomly generated dungeon indefinitely, resting after every fight until nothing is dangerous, and Michael Toy, Glenn Wichman and Ken Arnold needed pressure that could not be waited out. Hunger was cheap to implement, thematically invisible, and it made continuing the descent mandatory rather than merely advisable.

Anti-camping pressure is the durable idea, and it still underpins survival and roguelike design decades later. Badly tuned needs are also among the most complained-about systems in that space, because a meter emptying faster than the world supplies food becomes an errand rather than a threat. Better implementations make eating incidental to something the player already wanted to do, such as cooking, farming or exploring.

originDeveloper.name: Michael Toy, Glenn Wichman, Ken Arnold

f_class_system.name: Character Classes
f_class_system.summary: Character classes bundle abilities, restrictions and a role into a single early choice, trading a character's breadth for a clear identity and a defined place within a group.
prose: Choosing a class fixes what a character can equip, learn and do well, and often what they can never do at all. Design intent is complementarity, so a party or team needs several classes to cover its weaknesses, and the choice becomes a social contract as much as a build. Restrictions do the work, since a class is defined less by its abilities than by what it is forbidden.

Sir-Tech's Wizardry: Proving Grounds of the Mad Overlord in 1981 put a six-character party of distinct classes into a dungeon crawl, importing the structure from tabletop role-playing. Computers made the bookkeeping practical and the restrictions absolute, since software will not negotiate the way a game master does. Party format also solved a fairness problem, letting one player run a group whose members are deliberately incomplete alone.

Classes survive because they compress a large space of options into a legible decision, which matters more as audiences broaden. Same logic reappears as the shooter's loadout, the MOBA's champion and the hero shooter's roster. Cost is rigidity and the balance problem that follows, since every class must be viable without dominating, and players who want to build freely find the walls arbitrary. Hybrid systems keep attempting both.

f_los_detection.name: Line-of-Sight Detection
f_los_detection.summary: Line-of-sight detection gives enemies a limited field of view, so they can fail to notice a player, and the game starts tracking what its characters know separately from what is true.
prose: Each guard carries a facing and a cone or radius of vision, and detection becomes a question of geometry: where the player stands, what lies between them, whether the guard has turned. Sightlines break on walls, cover, distance and darkness. Because knowledge is held per character rather than globally, one room can contain several conflicting beliefs about it, and manipulating those beliefs is the actual gameplay.

Muse Software built Castle Wolfenstein in 1981 around guards who could be avoided rather than only fought, a pointed idea when most games modelled opponents as pursuers that always knew the player's position. Memory constraints helped, since a facing and a short check are cheap. Design intent mattered more: a game about escaping a fortress needs enemies whose attention is a resource to be managed.

An entire genre followed, along with a broader principle that combat can be a failure state rather than a goal. Legibility and fragility are the costs. Players cannot see a vision cone unless the game draws one, so detections often feel unfair, and such systems break memorably when a guard spots a body through a wall or forgets a firefight. Modern versions spend heavily on communicating what enemies perceive.

adoptedBy.name: Metal Gear Solid 4: Guns of the Patriots

f_flight_sim.name: Flight Simulation
f_flight_sim.summary: Flight simulation models aerodynamics, instruments and navigation for their own sake, offering no score and no enemy, on the argument that operating the aircraft correctly is itself the entertainment.
prose: Systems are the content. Lift and drag respond to airspeed and attitude, instruments read from the simulated state rather than from a heads-up display, and a flight consists of checklists, navigation between real airfields, radio procedure and a landing that either works or does not. Failure is rarely dramatic; it is being lost, low on fuel, or descending at a rate the airframe will not forgive.

subLOGIC's product line reached IBM personal computers as Microsoft Flight Simulator 1.0 in 1982, though the lineage runs back further, through earlier subLOGIC releases on 8-bit home machines and flight models written for mainframes. Choosing an unscored simulation was partly a hardware argument: drawing a wireframe world and integrating flight equations consumed everything the machine had, leaving nothing for adversaries or scoring systems.

Simulation as its own reward established a whole branch of the medium, with a hardware ecosystem of yokes and pedals and an audience that treats fidelity as the review criterion. That audience is also a constraint, because every increase in realism narrows the potential player base. Its tradition has survived through study-level products and by supplying the flight models that action games then simplify for everyone else.

f_iso_view.name: Isometric Projection
f_iso_view.summary: Isometric projection draws a world at a fixed oblique angle so that height, width and depth are all visible at once, while the underlying data stays a flat two-dimensional grid.
prose: Tiles and sprites are drawn as parallelograms at a constant angle, usually with no perspective foreshortening, and objects are sorted back to front so nearer things overlap farther ones. Since the camera never rotates, every asset can be drawn once by hand, and the world remains a grid the code can reason about. Trade-offs show up as ambiguity about exact height, occlusion behind tall objects, and diagonal movement that fights the controls.

Sega's Zaxxon in 1982 flew a ship over a fortress rendered at an angle, using shadows to communicate altitude in a space where nothing else could. Same-year arcade games such as Q*bert reached for the projection too, so the exact first is debatable; what Zaxxon showed was that the angle could carry gameplay information rather than just decoration. Drawing at a slant cost nothing extra on 2D sprite hardware.

Projection became the default for games that need to show a lot of state at once: cities, battle lines, dungeon floors and party positions all read better from above and to the side than from eye level. Real 3D never displaced it, because a fixed angle guarantees readability and consistent art. What it gives up is intimacy and precise spatial judgment, which is why action games mostly left it behind.

adoptedBy.name: Dune II: The Building of a Dynasty
Super Mario RPG: Legend of the Seven Stars
Baldur's Gate II: Shadows of Amn

f_parallax.name: Parallax Depth Layers
f_parallax.summary: Parallax depth layers scroll background planes more slowly than the foreground, producing a convincing impression of distance on hardware that has no concept of depth at all.
prose: Scenery is split into two or more planes. Foreground tiles move at the speed of the player, a middle band at some fraction of it, and a far band barely at all. Because the eye reads slower motion as greater distance, a flat image acquires a rough sense of depth. Cost is mostly memory and bandwidth rather than computation, and the effect breaks the moment a background object needs to be touched.

Irem's Moon Patrol in 1982 is the usual credit, with three bands of lunar hills sliding past at different rates behind a buggy. Attribution is contested, and the 1981 arcade game Jump Bug is frequently named earlier. What is not in doubt is why the technique spread: it bought visible production value from spare tile layers, and consoles of the following decade shipped multiple scrolling planes as a hardware feature.

Depth layers gave 2D games atmosphere and scale without changing anything about how they play, which is exactly the appeal and the limitation. Backgrounds became mood rather than space, a place for weather, cities and skylines the player can never reach. Because parallax is purely presentational, it survived the arrival of 3D as a stylistic choice, and side-scrolling games still use it to signal size and speed.

f_scaling_pseudo3d.name: Sprite-Scaling Pseudo-3D
f_scaling_pseudo3d.summary: Sprite-scaling pseudo-3D enlarges and repositions flat images as they approach the viewer, producing convincing forward motion on hardware with no ability to render three-dimensional geometry of its own.
prose: Objects are stored as sprites with a scale factor tied to their distance along a track or corridor. A road is drawn as a stack of horizontal bands whose width and curvature shift each frame, and roadside objects are stamped in at a size derived from their place in the queue. Nothing exists in three dimensions; there is a single depth value driving a lookup, which is why the camera can never leave the rail.

Namco's Pole Position in 1982 put a driver behind a scaling road with curves, opponents and a qualifying lap. Sega's Turbo from 1981 is often cited earlier, and the technique arrived through custom scaling hardware rather than a single insight, so the origin reads better as a line than a point. Reason for its dominance was economic: scaling silicon was cheap, and polygon rendering at arcade frame rates was not.

Rails made a decade of spectacle possible: racers, rail shooters and cockpit games that feel fast because sprites swell rather than because anything is simulated. Limits are severe and obvious in hindsight. Nothing can be approached from an unplanned angle, geometry cannot be intersected, and the illusion collapses the moment a player wants to leave the road. Polygonal hardware retired the technique, then style brought it back.

f_level_editor.name: Bundled Level Editor
f_level_editor.summary: A bundled level editor ships the authoring tool inside the game itself, letting players build, save and share their own levels from exactly the pieces the original designer used.
prose: Tools sit in the menu beside the campaign. Players place platforms, enemies, items and exits on the same grid the shipped levels use, test immediately, and save the result. Because the editor writes the format the game reads, a player-made level is indistinguishable from an official one, and distribution becomes a matter of passing a file to somebody else by whatever means exist.

Douglas E. Smith included an editor with Lode Runner in 1983, when a level was a grid layout and the tool that produced the shipped levels had already been written. Home computers arrived with an expectation that owners would type and create rather than only consume. Shipping the editor therefore cost very little and converted a fixed set of a hundred and fifty levels into an open-ended one.

Players became designers without asking permission, and the pipeline from making levels to making games has run through this door ever since. Quality control and support are the costs, since most user levels are poor and the good ones need to be findable, which is why later systems added ratings and curation. Editors also constrain, because a level built from a game's pieces can only argue within them.

f_day_night.name: Day/Night Cycle
f_day_night.summary: A day and night cycle advances a world clock independently of the player, changing light, behaviour and available activity, so time passes whether or not anyone is doing anything with it.
prose: A clock runs at a fixed ratio to real time. Lighting and colour follow it, and other systems subscribe: shops open and close, certain creatures appear only after dark, crops grow, festivals arrive on schedule. Most games also provide a way to skip ahead by sleeping or resting, which is a quiet admission that the cycle is both an atmospheric device and an obstacle players will want to route around.

Origin Systems put a working clock into Ultima III: Exodus in 1983, when home machines could barely afford to track anything the player was not looking at. Doing so was cheap in memory and enormous in implication, because a world with its own time is a world that exists while unobserved. Tabletop and mainframe designs had tracked time before, so what changed was making it visible and consequential.

Independent time is the foundation under schedules, weather, farming and survival systems, and it remains one of the cheapest ways to make a space feel inhabited. Costs are mostly friction: night is darker and therefore harder to read, timed content can be missed entirely, and waiting is rarely interesting, so designers have spent four decades inventing ways to let players skip the thing they added.

f_qte.name: Quick-Time Event
f_qte.summary: A quick-time event asks for a specific input at a specific moment during an otherwise non-interactive sequence, reducing participation to timing while the spectacle plays out as authored.
prose: Prompt appears, a short window opens, and the correct button either continues the sequence or triggers a failure branch. Player has no positional control and no strategy, only recognition and reaction. Design value is that any authored animation, however complex, can be made participatory at almost no cost, which is why the technique attaches to scenes that would be impossible to build as real gameplay.

Dragon's Lair, produced by Advanced Microcomputer Systems in 1983, ran hand-drawn animation from a laserdisc, a medium that could play film but could not render anything. Only possible interaction was choosing which pre-filmed segment played next, so the game became a series of timed inputs against gorgeous footage. Term itself came later, from Shenmue, but the structure was fixed in the arcade in 1983.

Cheapness explains its persistence, since a studio can make a cinematic moment interactive by adding a prompt rather than a system. Same cheapness explains the contempt, because the input rarely expresses anything about the player beyond attention, and failure repeats a scene already watched. Modern use is mostly narrow, either as a deliberate gesture in interactive drama or as punctuation inside a real combat system.

adoptedBy.name: Super Mario RPG: Legend of the Seven Stars

f_checkpoint.name: Checkpoint Respawn
f_checkpoint.summary: Checkpoint respawn returns a failed player to a marked point inside the level rather than to the beginning, making failure a small setback instead of a session-ending loss.
prose: Game records a position and a subset of world state at defined moments, then restores that snapshot on death. Where the markers sit, and what they restore, sets a game's actual difficulty far more than enemy statistics do. Frequent checkpoints turn a hard sequence into a drill; distant ones make the same sequence an endurance test, and that choice determines whether failure teaches or simply punishes.

Activision's Pitfall II: Lost Caverns in 1984 replaced lives entirely with checkpoint crosses in a large underground map, an unusual decision for an era of arcade-derived design. Cartridge games were being played at home, where no coin box set the pace and a long exploratory level needs some way to be attempted repeatedly. Removing the game-over screen was as significant as adding the marker.

Checkpointing is the main reason modern games can be both difficult and finishable, and its granularity is now a tuning knob applied sequence by sequence. It also changed what difficulty means, shifting it from resource attrition toward execution under repetition. Critics note that near-instant respawn removes the weight of dying, and designers respond with penalties, from lost currency to spent resources, that restore cost without ending the run.

adoptedBy.name: Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time

f_cutscene.name: In-Engine Cutscene
f_cutscene.summary: An in-engine cutscene takes control away and uses the game's own graphics to stage a scene, so story and play share one set of characters, one world and one visual language.
prose: Engine drives characters through scripted actions while input is ignored or reduced, then hands control back. Because the same assets are used, a scene can cut to a location the player will later occupy, or show an antagonist doing something elsewhere. Length and frequency are the design levers, and the crucial question is always what a scene does that the playable portion could not have done instead.

Jordan Mechner's Karateka in 1984 cut between the approaching hero and events inside the fortress, including a princess and a captor the player had not yet met. Technique came from cinema literacy applied to an 8-bit computer, and it worked because rotoscoped animation was expressive enough to carry a moment without text. Nothing extra had to be stored, since the scenes reused the game's own sprites and backgrounds.

Scenes became the default way games deliver plot, and the argument about them started almost immediately, since taking the controller is the one thing an interactive medium is uniquely able not to do. Costs are concrete too, because cutscenes consume budget, resist localisation and interrupt pacing. Every later technique, from full-motion video to fully playable dialogue, is a response to the same unsolved tension.

adoptedBy.name: Wing Commander III: Heart of the Tiger

f_seeded_universe.name: Seeded Procedural Universe
f_seeded_universe.summary: A seeded procedural universe stores no world at all, deriving planets, names, economies and positions from one starting number, so the same seed always reproduces exactly the same galaxy.
prose: Instead of data, the game holds an algorithm and a seed. Running that seed through a deterministic sequence produces coordinates, planet names, government types, technology levels and trade prices, and running it again reproduces them precisely. Nothing needs saving because nothing was ever stored. Scale becomes a function of arithmetic rather than of disk space, and a seed shared between two machines yields identical worlds on both.

David Braben and Ian Bell wrote Elite in 1984 for home computers with kilobytes of memory, where storing thousands of star systems was flatly impossible. Their generator produced far more galaxies than the game shipped with, and the pair cut the number deliberately on the reasoning that eight was already more than anyone would visit. Constraint dictated the technique, and the technique then dictated what kind of game could exist.

Vast spaces became cheap, which permanently raised the ambitions of space and survival games and turned the seed itself into something players trade. Uniformity is the cost. A million systems from one formula are a million variations on a single idea, and the real labour shifts to making that variety mean something. Later games mix generated bulk with authored landmarks for exactly this reason.

f_split_screen.name: Split-Screen Simultaneous
f_split_screen.summary: Split-screen play divides one display into separate viewports, so players sharing a room can occupy different parts of the same world, each seeing only what their own character sees.
prose: Rendering happens twice. Each viewport runs its own camera over shared world state, which roughly doubles drawing cost and forces compromises in resolution, draw distance and effects. Design gains what rendering loses, because players can now separate, hide, ambush and lie when information is no longer shared. Looking at the other half of the screen is cheating that nobody can prevent and everybody does.

First Star Software released Spy vs Spy in 1984 with a split display that let two players sabotage each other inside the same building without knowing where the other one was. Its comic-strip premise depended on hidden traps, which is impossible when both players share a camera. Doubling the rendering load was affordable precisely because the graphics were simple, a trade every split-screen game has repeated since.

Asymmetric information between people in the same room is a specific social pleasure, and it carried console multiplayer for two decades. Technical cost eventually killed it, since rendering four views became expensive as fidelity rose and online play removed the need. Its disappearance is a recurring complaint from players, and several studios have restored split-screen as a deliberate feature rather than an assumed default.

f_branching_dialogue.name: Branching Dialogue Trees
f_branching_dialogue.summary: Branching dialogue trees present conversation as a set of chosen replies, each one opening or closing later options, turning talk into something the player navigates rather than watches.
prose: A dialogue tree is a graph. Each node holds a line of NPC speech and a list of player responses; picking one moves you to another node, and some nodes set flags that alter what is available later or elsewhere. Early implementations used typed keywords rather than menus, so the branching was hidden inside a vocabulary the player had to assemble from rumours, letters and overheard names.

Origin Systems built the technique into Ultima IV: Quest of the Avatar in 1985 because the game needed to test the player's ethics, and a test demands questions with answers. Conversation was the only interface capable of asking. Attribution is genuinely contested: text adventures had accepted typed input for years, and other role-playing games of the period experimented with keyword talk, so Ultima IV is best read as the point where dialogue became a designed structure rather than a parser trick.

Consequences run in two directions. Writing became combinatorial, so cost grew with every branch, and studios learned to fake width with options that quietly converge inside a single scene. Set against that, dialogue trees gave the medium a way to make players responsible for what their character says, which is the precondition for reputation systems, companion relationships and endings that actually differ. Critics have argued ever since that picking from a list is not the same as speaking.

origin.name: Ultima IV: Quest of the Avatar

f_morality_axis.name: Explicit Morality Axis
f_morality_axis.summary: An explicit morality axis scores the player's behaviour on a visible ethical scale, then uses that number to unlock powers, change how characters react, and decide which ending appears.
prose: Behaviour gets measured. Actions carry stated or hidden weights, a counter moves toward one pole or another, and thresholds gate abilities, prices, dialogue and endings. Implementations vary enormously in granularity: some track several named virtues independently, others collapse everything onto one good-and-evil slider with two colour-coded buttons per conversation. Nearly all of them expose the score somewhere in the interface, which changes how people play the moment they notice it.

Ultima IV: Quest of the Avatar shipped in 1985 with an unusual problem to solve. Origin Systems wanted a role-playing game with no villain, in which the goal was to become a moral exemplar, and tracking eight virtues was the only way to make that goal checkable by a computer. Richard Garriott has described the design as a reply to criticism of his earlier games, where players were free to rob and murder townspeople at no cost.

Scoring ethics makes them tractable and shallow at the same time. Once players learn that generosity pays, the axis stops measuring morality and starts measuring optimisation, which is why so many games funnel people into playing consistently saintly or consistently monstrous rather than inconsistently human. Designers have spent decades trying to escape that trap, mostly by replacing the single axis with faction standing, or by refusing to show the number at all.

f_precision_platform.name: Momentum-Based Platform Control
f_precision_platform.summary: Momentum-based platform control gives an avatar acceleration, skidding and a jump whose height depends on how long the button is held, making movement itself a skill worth learning.
prose: Instead of moving a fixed number of pixels per frame, the character accumulates velocity, keeps it when direction changes, and sheds it gradually through friction. Jump height varies with how long the button stays down, and control in the air is partial rather than total. Consequences are felt immediately: stopping takes planning, a running start changes what is reachable, and identical inputs produce different results depending on state.

Nintendo R&D4 built Super Mario Bros. in 1985 around a single character who had to stay expressive across a very large number of screens, with only a directional pad and two buttons available. Physics answered that problem cheaply. A handful of tuned constants for acceleration, friction and gravity produced a movement vocabulary rich enough to fill a game, and level design could then be written against the shape of the jump arc.

Tuned movement turned platformers into games about a relationship with a body rather than about routes, which is why players argue about feel in terms usually reserved for instruments. It also raised the barrier to entry, since a character that slides is harder to control than one that stops instantly, and it made ports and emulation sensitive to frame timing. Later designers treat these constants as the genre's real content.

adoptedBy.name: Commander Keen in Invasion of the Vorticons

f_metroidvania.name: Ability-Gated Interlocked Map
f_metroidvania.summary: An ability-gated interlocked map is one continuous world whose closed routes open only when the player gains a new capability, so progress is measured in movement options rather than levels cleared.
prose: World is authored as a single connected space, then seeded with obstacles that specific abilities defeat: a high ledge, a narrow gap, a sealed door. Since the player can go anywhere the current toolkit permits, the map doubles as a quest log, and a remembered obstacle becomes a task. Designers control pacing by controlling access, and backtracking turns into a reward, because old rooms read differently once new powers exist.

Nintendo R&D1 released Metroid in 1986 on a cartridge that had to hold a large world in very little space. Reuse solved that: the same corridors are crossed repeatedly in different states, so the content budget goes into connections rather than new rooms. A non-linear map also suited the game's isolation, since a player free to wander is a player who can get lost, which was precisely the intended feeling.

Structure proved durable because it converts exploration into progression without any external progress bar, and it lets a designer sequence a story using geography. Failure modes are equally durable. Players stall when a gate is unmemorable, maps become chores to re-walk, and ability sets converge on the same double jump and dash. Argument over whether the form needs combat at all is still very much live.

adoptedBy.name: The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past

f_battery_save.name: Battery-Backed Save File
f_battery_save.summary: Battery-backed saving puts a small amount of powered memory inside the cartridge so a game can record its own state, allowing play to be suspended and resumed at will.
prose: Cartridge carries RAM and a coin cell that keeps it alive when the console is off, plus logic to write and verify a save file. Because the game controls what is written, it can store far more than a password could carry, including world flags, inventories, positions and multiple slots. Fragility is physical: batteries expire after years, and a dead cell erases a file that exists nowhere else.

Nintendo R&D4 shipped The Legend of Zelda in 1986 with battery memory, in a game explicitly designed around exploring a large world across many sessions. Hardware cost was the obstacle, since a battery raises the price of every cartridge, and the decision only makes sense for a game whose length is the point. Multiple save slots also made the console a shared household object rather than a personal one.

Saving invented the campaign as we now understand it: stories that unfold over dozens of hours, worlds that remember, and progress belonging to a player rather than to a session. It also created a class of design problems games still argue about, including where saving is allowed, whether it can be used to undo mistakes, and what it means when a game deliberately withholds or manipulates the file.

f_password_save.name: Password Continuation
f_password_save.summary: Password continuation encodes a player's progress as a string of characters they write down, letting a game remember its state without any storage hardware inside the cartridge.
prose: State is packed into a bit field, obscured, and printed as letters and numbers; typing it back reconstructs the game's variables. Length of the password is a direct measure of how much the game remembers, and designers economise by discarding details such as exact position or partial inventory. Since the code is data, invented or mistyped passwords sometimes produce valid but unintended states, which players quickly turned into a hobby.

Nintendo R&D1 used the technique in Metroid in 1986 for a game far too long to finish in one sitting, on a cartridge with no memory to spare for saving. Passwords cost nothing but a little ROM and some arithmetic. Trade-off was accepted across the era, because the alternative was either an unreasonably short game or a battery, which added expense to every cartridge manufactured.

Portable state made long-form console games viable a generation before saving became standard, and it created an accidental culture: codes shared in magazines, traded in playgrounds, and discovered to unlock debug conditions their authors never advertised. Friction was the cost, since a transcription error erases an evening and nothing carries over that the designer chose not to encode. Batteries retired the format quickly once they became affordable.

f_expansion_pack.name: Retail Expansion Pack
f_expansion_pack.summary: Retail expansion packs sell extra campaigns, missions or systems for a game already owned, requiring the original to run and treating a released title as a platform for further product.
prose: Content ships as a separate purchase that depends on the base game: new missions, units, buildings, regions or rules, usually made with the same tools by the same team. Save data often carries across. Pricing sits below a full release, and because the pack is built for people who finished the original, it can assume knowledge and open at a difficulty no standalone game would dare.

Origin Systems released Wing Commander: The Secret Missions in 1990, a set of new missions running on the existing engine, and it is commonly cited as the first true expansion pack. Earlier scenario and data disks for wargames and adventure games complicate that claim. Economics drove it either way, since the engine represented most of the development cost and reusing it converted a finished product into a second revenue event.

Games stopped being finished objects and became product lines, a shift that made long-lived franchises viable and gave studios work between releases. Fragmentation is one cost, as multiplayer populations split between owners and non-owners, and temptation is another, since content nearly complete at launch can always be held back. Every later model, from downloadable content to seasonal passes, argues with the precedent set here.

adoptedBy.name: Elden Ring: Shadow of the Erdtree

f_mode7_plane.name: Rotating Ground Plane
f_mode7_plane.summary: A rotating ground plane is a single texture-mapped floor that hardware can scale and spin one scanline at a time, letting a 2D console show a surface the player appears to drive across.
prose: One large bitmap is treated as a floor and sampled row by row, with each scanline reading the texture at a different scale and angle. Result is a plane that can rotate around the camera and recede toward a horizon, all without polygons. Everything above the floor is still a sprite, so buildings, vehicles and scenery stay flat, and the illusion depends on keeping the viewer low and close to the ground.

Nintendo EAD's F-Zero launched with the Super Nintendo in 1990 and was built to demonstrate the console's affine background mode. Racing was a natural fit, since a track is mostly floor and the camera stays low, which hides the technique's weaknesses. Hardware performed the transform for free on every scanline, so the game ran fast and smooth at a time when software 3D on home machines could do neither.

Effect of the trick was to make console racing and overhead flight feel three-dimensional years before dedicated 3D chips arrived, and it defined the look of a console generation. Constraints were strict: one plane, no elevation, no geometry to collide with, and poor results if the camera rises. Once polygons became cheap the technique turned into a period style rather than a working tool.

f_turn_grid_tactics.name: Turn-Based Grid Tactics
f_turn_grid_tactics.summary: Turn-based grid tactics play out on squares, each side moving a roster of individual units in sequence, with those units carrying experience, equipment and consequences from battle to battle.
prose: Movement is counted in tiles and bounded by terrain cost. Units alternate by side, attack from adjacent or ranged positions, and take advantages from height, cover, facing or weapon type. Persistence is what separates the form from a board game: characters level up, learn skills, form relationships and, in some designs, die permanently, so a decision made on one battlefield echoes through the remainder of the campaign.

Intelligent Systems released Fire Emblem: Shadow Dragon and the Blade of Light in 1990 on hardware that suited the form exactly. A grid is cheap to draw, turns need no processing headroom, and a console audience could take as long as it liked over a move. Combining wargame structure with role-playing progression gave individual soldiers names and histories, which is precisely what makes losing one land.

Two decades of tactical role-playing games follow from that merger, and the format survives because it scales down to modest hardware and up to considerable depth. Pace and punishment are the costs. Battles run long, one mistake can be irreversible where death is permanent, and reloading becomes the rational response, which many designs then legislate against with checkpoints or forgiving modes.

origin.name: Fire Emblem: Shadow Dragon and the Blade of Light

adoptedBy.name: Fire Emblem: Mystery of the Emblem
Heroes of Might and Magic III

f_weapon_durability.name: Weapon Durability Decay
f_weapon_durability.summary: Weapon durability decay makes equipment wear out with use, so tools become consumables on a budget rather than permanent possessions and the player keeps replacing whatever they fight with.
prose: Each item carries a use counter. Swinging, firing or blocking decrements it, and at zero the item breaks or becomes useless, sometimes with repair available at a price. Design consequences follow immediately: inventory turns into rotating stock rather than a museum, powerful finds get spent instead of hoarded, and a designer can hand the player something extraordinary without permanently flattening the difficulty curve behind it.

Intelligent Systems shipped Fire Emblem: Shadow Dragon and the Blade of Light in 1990 with durability because its units die permanently and its weapons form a triangle of counters. Limited uses stopped players solving every map with one legendary sword and forced rotation through characters and armaments. Constraint suited a strategy game in which each battle is a resource problem inside a campaign that never returns anything you spend.

Durability is among the most reliably disliked systems in the medium and among the most useful. Breakage creates improvisation, prevents hoarding, and keeps a difficulty curve honest; it also generates busywork, punishes attachment, and encourages players to save their best equipment for a moment that never comes. Where it works, replacement is fast and generous. Where it fails, repair becomes a chore performed in menus between fights.

origin.name: Fire Emblem: Shadow Dragon and the Blade of Light

adoptedBy.name: The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild
The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom

f_dynamic_music.name: Adaptive Dynamic Music
f_dynamic_music.summary: Adaptive dynamic music follows the player, transitioning between arrangements on musical boundaries so a score can change with the scene without cutting off or restarting a track.
prose: Music is stored as sequences with marked branch points rather than as a finished recording. When the game state changes, the system waits for the next musically sensible moment, then moves to a matching arrangement, adding instruments, shifting key, or crossing into a variation. Because transitions land on the beat, the score sounds composed rather than switched, and a theme can follow a character from room to room.

Lucasfilm Games shipped Monkey Island 2: LeChuck's Revenge in 1991 with an interactive music system built by the studio's own composers for exactly this problem. Adventure games created the need, since a player may stand in one room for a minute or twenty and the music has to survive both. Sequenced formats made it possible, because a score held as instructions can be rearranged in ways a recording cannot.

Scores stopped looping and started responding, which is now standard practice and has produced its own compositional discipline of layers, stems and vertical arrangement. Authorship pays for it. Music written to recombine must work in many orders, which limits long-form development, and a dynamic system can smear a strong cue into wallpaper. Composers still argue about how much control to hand over to a state machine.

f_combo_string.name: Chained Combo Strings
f_combo_string.summary: Chained combo strings are attack sequences timed so each hit lands while the opponent is still reeling from the last, making the rest of the run unblockable once the first connects.
prose: Hit reaction is the mechanism. A connecting attack puts the target in a stun state lasting a fixed number of frames, and an attack begun inside that window arrives before the defender regains control. Chaining therefore depends on frame data rather than on any dedicated combo mode, and skill lies in knowing which moves recover fast enough to link, which is why the technique produced deep, memorised notation among competitive players.

Capcom did not design it. While finishing Street Fighter II: The World Warrior in 1991 the team noticed that cancelling the recovery of one move into another let hits connect in sequence, judged the timing too demanding for most players to exploit, and left it alone. Players found it within weeks. Combos consequently arrived as a discovered property of the engine rather than a feature, which is unusually well documented for a bug.

Strings gave fighting games a skill ceiling nobody had authored, splitting the audience between players who drill execution and players who do not, and setting off thirty years of balancing between them. Outside the genre, the same idea became the grammar of character action games, skateboarding scoring and superhero brawlers, where a string matters less for damage than for rhythm and spectacle. Combo breakers and bursts have been arriving ever since.

origin.name: Street Fighter II: The World Warrior

adoptedBy.name: Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time

f_4x_empire.name: Turn-Based 4X Empire
f_4x_empire.summary: Turn-based 4X games ask players to explore, expand, exploit and exterminate across a map and a timeline, growing a civilisation from one settler into an empire over hundreds of turns.
prose: Play spans scales that other genres keep separate. Cities are founded and specialised, terrain is improved, research advances a technology tree, diplomacy and war run alongside trade, and a single turn may cover a decade. Victory conditions are plural, including conquest, science and culture, so one map supports incompatible strategies. Decisions compound slowly, which makes an early choice about where to settle unusually heavy.

Sid Meier and Bruce Shelley built Sid Meier's Civilization at MicroProse in 1991, drawing on board wargames, city-building software and earlier historical simulations. Turn-based structure was partly a practical necessity, since simulating a world in real time was out of reach, but it also matched the subject. History is a sequence of decisions with long consequences, and a turn is a reasonable unit for one of them.

History became something a player argues with rather than reads, and the genre's grip is famous enough to have generated its own vocabulary about lost evenings. Consequences are political too, because any model of civilisation encodes claims about progress, colonisation and violence that later designers have revisited deliberately. Late-game tedium remains the persistent design problem, since a won game still demands hours of administration.

adoptedBy.name: Heroes of Might and Magic III

f_fog_of_war.name: Fog of War
f_fog_of_war.summary: Fog of war hides any part of a map that no friendly unit can currently see, making information a contested resource and turning scouting into a requirement rather than an option.
prose: Terrain stays hidden until visited, and once explored it often persists as a remembered snapshot that no longer updates, so a base seen ten minutes ago may be a lie. Units project a vision radius that travels with them. Everything outside it is unknown: enemy positions, army composition, expansions. Producing vision therefore costs resources, and denying it, through terrain, cloaking or high ground, becomes a tactic in its own right.

Westwood Studios used the mechanic in Dune II in 1992 as the real-time strategy template took shape, though hidden-map play was already familiar from earlier computer wargames and from the board wargames those descended from. Necessity helped. An opponent whose entire build is visible gives nobody a reason to scout, and a real-time game with perfect information collapses into arithmetic. Concealment also flatters simple artificial intelligence by hiding its behaviour.

Scouting, deception and the timing attack all descend from this one restriction, and it is why strategy games have a metagame at all. Costs fall on spectators and newcomers, who cannot see why a player is suddenly panicking, and on interface designers, who must communicate absence. Cheats that reveal the map are so destructive precisely because the entire genre rests on the assumption that knowledge is expensive.

origin.name: Dune II: The Building of a Dynasty

adoptedBy.name: Age of Empires II: The Age of Kings
Heroes of Might and Magic III

f_fmv.name: Full-Motion Video
f_fmv.summary: Full-motion video builds a game out of filmed actors stored on optical media, with the player choosing which pre-recorded footage plays next rather than controlling a rendered character.
prose: Footage is shot on a set with a cast and crew, compressed, and stored as clips that branch. Player input usually amounts to selecting a camera, a room or a moment of intervention, and the engine's job is to reach the next clip without a visible seam. Because every possible outcome must be filmed in advance, the design space is fixed on the shooting day and cannot be revised in code afterwards.

Digital Pictures released Night Trap in 1992, once CD-ROM drives gave home machines enough storage to hold video at all. Its material had been shot years earlier for a cartridge system that never shipped, which is part of why the credit is contested: laserdisc arcade cabinets had been playing branching filmed and animated sequences since the early 1980s, and several CD-ROM titles were in production simultaneously. What 1992 added was a mass-market console format.

Commercially the genre collapsed within about five years, killed by grainy compression, thin interaction and the arrival of convincing real-time 3D. Its residue is permanent, though: production values became a competitive axis, studios started hiring casting directors and composers, and the expectation that a game contains cinema outlived the technique that introduced it. Video also survived as a framing device, used for briefings, archive footage and deliberately artificial texture.

adoptedBy.name: Wing Commander III: Heart of the Tiger
Star Wars Jedi Knight: Dark Forces II

f_npc_schedules.name: NPC Daily Schedules
f_npc_schedules.summary: NPC daily schedules give characters routines of sleeping, working and eating tied to the world clock, so a town behaves like a society rather than a rank of stationary quest dispensers.
prose: Each character owns a timetable. Entries pair a time with a place and an activity, and pathfinding moves them between home, workplace, tavern and bed, with routines interrupted by events like rain, crime, or the player standing in a doorway. Because schedules are data rather than script, the simulation keeps running off screen, and anyone who arrives at the wrong hour finds a shop closed and a street empty.

Origin Systems shipped Ultima VII: The Black Gate in 1992 with a full town simulation of this kind, after several games spent building toward it. Memory and pathfinding had been the limiting factors, and by 1992 a personal computer could hold a city's worth of routines. Motivation was fictional as much as technical, since the plot is a murder investigation and investigation requires a world where people have habits.

Routines produce the impression of society cheaply, and they make theft, stealth and eavesdropping meaningful, because knowing when a room is empty is real knowledge. Costs appear as fragility and friction: characters get stuck, schedules break under crowd conditions, quest givers wander off mid-conversation, and players spend real minutes waiting outside a locked door for a shopkeeper who is asleep exactly as designed.

adoptedBy.name: The Legend of Zelda: Majora's Mask

f_raycast_3d.name: Raycast Corridor 3D
f_raycast_3d.summary: Raycast corridor 3D draws a first-person view by casting one ray per screen column into a flat grid of walls, producing textured corridors fast enough to run on ordinary office computers.
prose: Level is a two-dimensional grid of solid or empty cells.
