For each vertical column of pixels the renderer casts a ray until it strikes a wall, uses the distance to decide how tall that column should be, and samples a texture to fill it. Floors and ceilings are flat colours or simple planes, everything else is a scaled sprite, and walls share one height with no rooms above rooms.

id Software shipped Wolfenstein 3D in 1992 on PC hardware with no graphics acceleration, where general 3D rendering was hopeless but a tightly constrained special case was not. Restricting the world to a grid removed almost all of the mathematics, and the studio had rehearsed the approach in earlier titles including Catacomb 3-D. Distribution mattered as much as the renderer, since shareware put a fast first-person game on machines bought for spreadsheets.

Speed was the whole argument. A first-person view running at a responsive frame rate turned the viewpoint from a curiosity into an action genre, and it set expectations for movement, weapons and level flow that persist. Grid geometry also limited what those levels could say, because a world of right angles and equal heights cannot describe a real place. Every later renderer was an attempt to lift that restriction.

f_rts_base.name: Real-Time Base and Unit Production
f_rts_base.summary: Real-time base building has players harvest resources, raise production buildings and field armies under continuous time pressure, with no turns and every task competing for the same attention.
prose: One loop drives everything: gather a resource, spend it on buildings, buildings produce units, units take ground and protect the harvesters. Time never stops, so construction and combat compete for attention and for the same income. Units are selected with a mouse and ordered directly, production queues run in the background, and a technology tree gates stronger options behind earlier buildings.

Westwood Studios assembled the template in Dune II in 1992, drawing on earlier real-time experiments and on the mouse-driven interface home computers had recently standardised. Its licence supplied a setting where resource harvesting was already the fiction. Consolidation rather than invention was the achievement: sidebar production, direct unit selection, a harvest economy and a technology tree arranged into a shape that finally worked.

Nearly every strategy game since has argued with that arrangement, by extending it, stripping the base out, or collapsing the whole thing onto a single unit. Costs are baked into the format. Real-time play rewards mechanical speed as much as judgement, the opening minutes are usually a memorised routine, and a match can be decided by an economic lead long before anything visible happens.

origin.name: Dune II: The Building of a Dynasty

adoptedBy.name: Age of Empires II: The Age of Kings

f_immersive_sim.name: Systemic Solution Space
f_immersive_sim.summary: Systemic solution spaces build a game from consistent interacting rules rather than authored answers, so problems can be solved in ways the designers never anticipated and never wrote down.
prose: Rules are general rather than local. Objects have physical properties, characters have senses and allegiances, fire spreads, water conducts, and a key is one option among several. Because those rules apply everywhere instead of only where a designer expected them, a locked door might be opened, bypassed through a window, avoided entirely, or made irrelevant by persuading someone else to open it. Designers author obstacles; solutions emerge.

Blue Sky Productions built Ultima Underworld: The Stygian Abyss in 1992 as a first-person role-playing game with real geometry, physical objects and characters who could be talked to rather than only fought. Ambition rather than constraint drove the work, and the studio's later projects carried the approach forward. Its founding promise is a contract: if something looks like it should work, the simulation ought to honour the attempt.

Games built this way produce a strong sense of ownership, because a solution the player invented feels like theirs, and they support replaying in ways linear designs cannot. Severe costs explain the small output. Interacting systems generate bugs and unwinnable states, testing is combinatorial, and much of what gets built is never seen by any one player. Commercial results have been inconsistent enough that studios keep abandoning the form.

adoptedBy.name: Ultima Underworld II: Labyrinth of Worlds

f_cancel_meter.name: Cancels and Super Meter
f_cancel_meter.summary: Cancels and a super meter let a player interrupt one move's animation with another and bank a resource earned through fighting, spending it on a decisive attack at a chosen moment.
prose: Two rules work together. Cancelling permits a move still in its animation to be overridden by another input, which is what makes long strings possible; the meter fills as you attack, block and take damage, and empties when spent on a special that is faster, safer or far more damaging. Because the bar is visible to both players, everyone watching the cabinet can see when a round has turned dangerous.

Capcom formalised the pairing in Super Street Fighter II Turbo, after players had spent years exploiting cancels the studio never intended. Attribution is shared rather than clean: SNK fighters of the early 1990s had already experimented with drainable spirit gauges, and competing arcade boards were converging on similar ideas. What Capcom fixed in place was the loop in which playing well earns the resource that ends the round.

Meters gave the genre its comeback drama and much of its spectator legibility, which matters for a form watched over a shoulder or on a stream. They also shifted matches toward resource management, so a player behind on health may be ahead on options, and they made balance considerably harder, since a single meter-spending move has to be worth its cost without erasing the preceding two minutes of play.

f_automap.name: In-Game Automap
f_automap.summary: An in-game automap draws the level as the player walks it, converting movement into a persistent overhead diagram of rooms, corridors and doors that can be consulted at any moment.
prose: Geometry a player has seen is recorded and drawn from above as lines, usually on a toggled overlay with position and facing marked. Unvisited space stays blank, so the map is a record of where someone has been rather than a plan of where to go. Later versions annotate heavily: door colours, item pickups, room names, boss locations, and in some games marks the player places by hand.

id Software shipped one in Doom in 1993, at a point when levels had outgrown what a player could hold in memory. Corridors looped, keys sat behind doors two rooms back, and people were drawing grids on graph paper, a habit inherited from dungeon crawlers. Ultima Underworld had already offered an in-fiction map the year before, so the idea was in circulation. Doom supplied a fast, legible version bound to one key.

Externalising spatial memory made large, non-linear levels viable for players who would otherwise get lost and stop, and it turned the map itself into a design surface: completion percentages, rooms visible but unreachable, the shape of a world readable at a glance. Something was lost too. Attention to landmarks stopped being necessary, and a player's mental model of a space now often lives on the overlay rather than in their head.

adoptedBy.name: Ultima Underworld II: Labyrinth of Worlds
The Legend of Zelda: A Link Between Worlds

f_lan_deathmatch.name: Networked Deathmatch
f_lan_deathmatch.summary: Networked deathmatch connects several machines over a local network so players fight each other inside the same simulated level, replacing computer opponents with people in the next room.
prose: Machines exchange state across a shared network. Early implementations were peer-to-peer, with every copy simulating the world and broadcasting positions and events, which only works when the network is fast, local and trusted. Rules were minimal: a level, weapons distributed across it, respawns, and a running count of kills. Nearly everything competitive shooters do today descends from that small set of arrangements.

id Software added networked play to Doom in 1993, and the word deathmatch comes from that team. Precedent exists and is worth naming: networked competitive games ran on mainframes and university systems through the 1970s, including maze shooters played between terminals. What Doom supplied was reach, because it ran on ordinary office hardware that companies had already bought for entirely different reasons.

Competitive personal-computer gaming effectively begins here, along with mods, custom levels and a considerable body of corporate network policy written specifically to stop it. Limits proved as instructive as capabilities: local networks are trusted and low-latency, so nothing in the design anticipated cheating, lag compensation or strangers, and the following decade of engineering went into making the same experience survive the public internet.

adoptedBy.name: Star Wars Jedi Knight: Dark Forces II

f_mod_sdk.name: Open Data Formats and Mod SDK
f_mod_sdk.summary: Open data formats and modding kits let players replace a game's levels, art and rules without its source code, treating the engine as a platform and the content as swappable files.
prose: Assets live in archives the game reads at runtime, so replacing an archive replaces the content: maps, textures, sounds, weapons, enemy behaviour. Documentation, or a community's reverse engineering of the format, lets outsiders write tools against it. Later engines formalise the arrangement with scripting languages and published development kits, and total conversions built this way can share nothing with the original except the executable.

id Software separated Doom's engine from its data in 1993 and, unusually for the period, took an encouraging position toward the editors that appeared within weeks; a source release followed later. Self-interest played a part, because a game people keep making things for keeps selling. Culture mattered as much, given founders who had come up modifying other people's software on shared machines.

Free apprenticeship at scale is the consequence. Whole genres arrived as mods before they arrived as products, and a generation of studios was staffed by people whose first work was unpaid content for someone else's engine. Ownership and labour are the costs. Value created by that work accrues mostly to the platform holder, moddable games carry support and cheating burdens, and studios often close the door once a title becomes commercially sensitive.

lineage.name: Open Data Formats and Mod SDK

f_difficulty_select.name: Selectable Difficulty
f_difficulty_select.summary: Selectable difficulty asks players, before they begin, how hard the game should be, then adjusts enemy damage, enemy counts, resources or forgiveness to match the setting they declared.
prose: Choosing a setting changes numbers behind the scenes and sometimes content itself: enemy health and damage, how much ammunition spawns, how many opponents appear, whether saving is restricted, whether one mistake ends a run. Names carry tone as much as information, and the hardest tiers are usually positioned as a claim rather than an option. Most implementations lock the choice at the start; many now allow changes mid-run.

id Software gave Doom five named skill levels in 1993, spanning a range wide enough that identical maps served both a first-time player and someone replaying for mastery. Economics pushed that way. A single set of levels had to satisfy an audience with wildly different experience, and building separate campaigns was out of the question, while placing extra enemies at higher settings cost almost nothing in level data.

Access and challenge stopped being the same axis, which widened who could finish a game without lowering its ceiling. Tuning absorbs the cost, since every tier needs testing and the middle one takes most of it, and a game built for four settings can end up sharply tuned for none of them. Certain works refuse the option entirely, arguing that a fixed contract is part of what they mean.

f_env_storytelling.name: Environmental Storytelling
f_env_storytelling.summary: Environmental storytelling places narrative information in the arrangement of a space itself, so that players learn what happened by reading rooms, bodies and debris instead of watching a scene.
prose: Nothing pauses. A barricaded door, a chalk message, a corpse holding a keycard next to an empty medical cabinet: each detail is an authored fact placed where movement will find it, and the player assembles a sequence of events from the residue. Good examples are legible without explanation and reward a second look; weak examples degenerate into scattered props that gesture at meaning without encoding anything a careful reader could reconstruct.

Looking Glass Technologies used the approach heavily in System Shock in 1994, partly out of necessity. Its station was a first-person space with no party members to talk to and no budget for cinematics, so the level itself had to carry the plot. Attribution is loose here, since adventure games and even early dungeon crawlers had staged meaningful scenery before; System Shock's claim rests on doing it systematically, across an entire connected location, as the primary narrative channel.

Making space the narrator lets a game tell stories without taking control away, which suits designs built around exploration and dread. Costs follow. Players who move quickly miss most of it, ambiguity is easy to mistake for depth, and by the 2010s critics were describing whole games as walking tours through the aftermath of more interesting events. Whether that critique lands depends on how much the arrangement rewards attention.

adoptedBy.name: The Last of Us Part II

f_audio_log.name: Found Audio Log
f_audio_log.summary: The found audio log is a recorded message left by an absent character, picked up as an item and played while the player keeps moving, delivering exposition without stopping the game.
prose: Recordings are placed as collectibles. Each holds a monologue, often part of a numbered series scattered across a location, and playback continues over ordinary movement and combat so the fiction advances while control stays with the player. Most implementations add a menu where logs can be replayed, which matters because dialogue heard during a firefight is dialogue half missed. Voices belong to people who are usually dead by the time you hear them.

System Shock introduced the device in 1994 as a direct consequence of its setting. Looking Glass Technologies had a research station full of corpses, a protagonist who wakes up alone, and no cutscene budget, so email logs from the dead crew became the only way to stage a cast that could not appear. Recording audio was also far cheaper than animating characters, which made the technique attractive long after the technical constraint had lifted.

Few narrative devices have been imitated this literally. Audio logs solved the problem of story in a first-person game so cleanly that they became a default, then a joke: an entire species of character who narrates their own doom into a recorder for no plausible reason. Defenders point out that the format survives because it works, letting writers control pace and mood while the player is free to keep playing.

f_voice_acting.name: Full Voice Performance
f_voice_acting.summary: Full voice performance means every line of dialogue in a game is recorded by an actor rather than displayed as text, making performance part of the writing itself.
prose: Recording everything changes the production pipeline more than the game. Scripts must be locked before studio time, actors are directed line by line without seeing the scene, and every branch of dialogue costs money whether or not most players hear it. Delivery carries information text cannot: hesitation, contempt, exhaustion. Lip-sync, subtitles and localisation all attach to the same asset, which is why voiced games ship with far larger content pipelines than their word counts suggest.

Origin Systems shipped Wing Commander III: Heart of the Tiger in 1994 with a fully performed cast, taking advantage of CD-ROM capacity and the studio's existing appetite for filmed material. Credit is shared rather than exclusive: several CD-ROM titles were adding speech in the same window, and arcade and adventure games had been using recorded lines in smaller quantities for years. What was new was voicing a long branching script end to end.

Consequences cut both ways. Performance raised the emotional ceiling and made silent protagonists feel like an authorial choice rather than a default, but it also froze scripts early, made late revisions expensive, and pushed studios toward fewer, shorter lines. Games with enormous branching text have often stayed partly voiced for exactly this reason, and a few have made a virtue of it by voicing only a narrator or a signature character.

origin.name: Wing Commander III: Heart of the Tiger

adoptedBy.name: Metal Gear Solid 2: Sons of Liberty
Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic
Professor Layton and the Curious Village
Ni no Kuni: Wrath of the White Witch

f_ng_plus.name: New Game Plus
f_ng_plus.summary: New Game Plus restarts a completed game while carrying the player's accumulated power forward, so a second run becomes a different experience rather than a repetition of the first.
prose: On finishing, a player may begin again with levels, equipment or abilities intact against unchanged or slightly rescaled opposition. Early encounters collapse, pacing accelerates, and attention moves to content the first run could not reach. Some designs use the mode to gate real material, hiding endings, bosses or explanations behind a second or third completion, which turns replay into an extension of the story rather than a bonus.

Square's Chrono Trigger in 1995 built the mode around a plot involving time travel and a set of multiple endings, most of which are reachable only by confronting the final boss at unusual points. Replay was therefore not a courtesy but the mechanism through which the game is fully seen. Cartridge memory and a battery made carrying a completed state across a fresh start technically straightforward.

Approach solved a genuine problem, since long games are expensive to make and expensive to replay, and it gives mastery somewhere to go once credits roll. Risks are familiar. A run where nothing threatens the player is a victory lap that quickly bores, so later designs scale enemies, add modifiers or introduce new rules. Where it works, it converts knowledge of a game into that game's next difficulty setting.

f_free_roam_3d.name: Analog Free-Roam 3D Movement
f_free_roam_3d.summary: Analog free-roam 3D movement lets a third-person character run in any direction at any speed through an open volume, with a camera that has to be designed as carefully as the character.
prose: Stick direction is interpreted relative to the camera rather than the world, so pushing forward means away from the viewer wherever the viewer happens to be. Character turns toward the chosen heading with its own momentum, and speed is proportional to how far the stick is pushed. Because the camera defines what forward means, the camera becomes part of the control scheme, and every reframing it performs is felt as an input problem.

Nintendo EAD's Super Mario 64 launched in 1996 alongside a controller with an analog stick, and it had to answer a question nobody had settled: how to move a character freely in a volume and still see. Solutions were invented in public. Camera lives on a virtual arm with collision, the player can nudge it, and level geometry is shaped so the interesting route and the readable angle agree.

Grammar established here still runs almost all third-person action games, and it made possible the open worlds, climbing systems and lock-on combat that followed. Price was paid in complexity: cameras fail, depth is hard to judge without shadows, and a jump that was trivially readable in profile becomes a guess. Decades of design work since have gone into hiding those problems rather than solving them outright.

adoptedBy.name: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time
Jak and Daxter: The Precursor Legacy
Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time
The Legend of Zelda: Twilight Princess

f_beat_match.name: Beat-Matched Input
f_beat_match.summary: Beat-matched input judges the player against a musical grid, scoring each press by how closely it lands on the beat rather than by whether the right button was chosen.
prose: Timing carries the entire judgement. Prompts appear in a pattern tied to the music, and a press is graded by its distance from the target moment, usually into a few named bands running from perfect down to miss. Performance then feeds back into the audio: a poor run degrades the track or the vocalist, a good one embellishes it, so the score and the scoring are one object.

NanaOn-Sha released PaRappa the Rapper in 1996 on a console with a disc drive, which finally made streamed music of decent quality practical. Masaya Matsuura came from music rather than games, and the design treats call-and-response rap as the interaction itself: the game performs a phrase, the player repeats it. Rhythm-scored play existed earlier in Japan, but this is the release that established the form commercially.

Time became the difficulty axis, which is unusually accessible, because the rules are audible and anyone who can nod along already understands the system. Latency and licensing are the costs. Audio and display delay must be measured and compensated or the game is simply unfair, and music rights make the genre expensive while quietly removing old titles from sale. Precision requirements also exclude some disabled players.

adoptedBy.name: Guitar Hero III: Legends of Rock

f_skill_tree.name: Branching Skill Tree
f_skill_tree.summary: A branching skill tree spends earned points on a diagram of connected abilities, where reaching a powerful option means investing in its prerequisites and therefore giving up other branches.
prose: Points arrive with levels and are spent on nodes arranged in dependency chains. Since points are finite, every allocation forecloses another, and the tree's shape communicates that cost visually before the player commits. Good trees make trade-offs legible and let a specialisation feel like a plan; weak ones present an illusion of choice, where most paths converge or a single branch is obviously superior to the rest.

Blizzard North's Diablo in 1996 gave each class a page of skills tied to levels, in a game built around repeated runs whose reason to start again is to build differently. Visual layout mattered as much as the mathematics, since a chart shows a possible future in a way a list of numbers cannot. Its sequel expanded this into the large synergy trees that most later implementations imitate.

Trees spread far beyond role-playing games because they attach a visible plan to any progression, which keeps players oriented across long sessions. Same ubiquity is the complaint: many trees are filler, offering percentage increases that change nothing about play, and a respec button quietly removes the opportunity cost that justified the structure. Designers now argue for smaller trees with fewer, sharper decisions instead.

f_loot_rarity.name: Colour-Coded Loot Rarity
f_loot_rarity.summary: Colour-coded loot rarity assigns each item a colour that signals its tier at a glance, turning evaluation into an instant read rather than a comparison of statistics.
prose: Item generation picks a rarity tier, then rolls properties within that tier's range, and the display colours the item's name accordingly. White is ordinary, blue better, gold or orange exceptional. Player learns the language in minutes and can then triage a floor of drops without opening anything. Colour also drives feeling directly, since the flash of an unusual tint is a reward delivered before its contents are known.

Blizzard North needed players to sort through enormous quantities of generated items in Diablo in 1996 without stopping to read, because the game's loop is killing and looting at speed. Colour is the cheapest possible interface for that, requiring no text, no icon and no localisation. Convention it established proved so effective that games in unrelated genres adopted the same palette without ever explaining it.

One-glance value became the medium's most portable interface convention and, in parallel, its most exploitable. Rarity colours make a randomised drop feel like an event, which is exactly the property loot boxes and gacha systems monetise, and the flash works whether the item beneath it matters or not. Designers who want players to read items rather than colours now have to work against the expectation.

f_fixed_cam.name: Fixed Cinematic Camera
f_fixed_cam.summary: Fixed cinematic cameras place a 3D scene under pre-authored viewpoints that cut as the player moves, giving a designer control over framing at the cost of the player's control over sight.
prose: Each room is assigned one or more static camera positions, often over prerendered backgrounds with only characters drawn in real time. Movement is relative to the character rather than the view, so a cut can reverse what a direction on the stick means. Designer decides exactly what is visible, when it appears and how much of the room is withheld, and the player has no way to look around a corner.

Capcom's Resident Evil in 1996 used the technique because early 3D hardware could not render a detailed mansion in real time, but it could composite characters over a still image. Constraint became the aesthetic. Angles borrowed from horror cinema, and a cut that reveals a corridor already occupied does work no monster animation can. Prerendered art also let environments look far better than the era's polygon budget allowed.

Framing control gave games their first reliable dread, and it survives wherever a designer wants authorship over what is seen. Costs are well documented: tank controls exist partly to survive the cuts, combat becomes imprecise when an enemy is off-frame, and modern audiences read the scheme as friction. Remakes tend to drop it for shoulder cameras, which is itself an argument about whether the frustration was the point.

f_analog_input.name: Graded Analog Input
f_analog_input.summary: Graded analog input reads how far a stick is pushed rather than whether a direction is pressed, so speed, angle and pressure all become things a player can express.
prose: Stick position is sampled as a pair of values with a dead zone near the centre and a curve mapping deflection to output. Character can therefore tiptoe, walk or sprint from one control, and a turn can be a slight adjustment rather than a snap to eight directions. Designers gain a continuous input channel and the obligation to decide how the curve feels, since that mapping is the game's handwriting.

Nintendo's 1996 controller for Super Mario 64 put an analog stick in the middle of a mass-market gamepad, because free movement in a 3D volume cannot be expressed with a digital pad. Analog controls existed long before, in flight yokes, paddles and home computer joysticks; what changed was that a whole console generation standardised on them, which made designing for graded input a default rather than a special case.

Continuous input made stealth speeds, driving lines, precise aim and expressive animation possible, and it eventually carried triggers, pressure and gyroscopes alongside it. It also created a category of problems: dead zones, drift, response curves and accessibility issues a digital pad never had. Some genres pointedly refuse it, since fighting games and precise platformers often prefer the certainty of a switch that is either closed or open.

adoptedBy.name: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time

f_hub_world.name: Hub-and-Spoke World Access
f_hub_world.summary: A hub-and-spoke world is a central space connecting outward to self-contained levels, letting players choose what to attempt next and returning them to the middle between attempts.
prose: Hub is a small persistent area holding entrances to larger discrete levels, plus whatever services the game offers. Levels are entered, completed in part, and exited back to the centre, and most can be revisited with new abilities or objectives. Because the hub is where progress is displayed and stored, it does work a menu would otherwise do, and gating becomes a question of which doors have opened.

Super Mario 64 in 1996 needed a way to present many independent 3D playgrounds without a level select screen, and Nintendo EAD used a castle. Paintings on its walls are level entrances, and stars collected inside unlock more of the building. Practical constraints supported the choice, since only one level had to be loaded at a time, and a hub gives the player somewhere to stand while the game changes underneath.

Choice of order is the real product. A hub lets a designer offer several routes without building a truly open world, keeps difficulty selectable without a difficulty menu, and gives repeated visits an emotional anchor. Weaknesses are equally familiar: hubs become long corridors between the parts people want, and their fiction often strains. Later games kept the structure while dressing it as a camp, a ship or a village.

adoptedBy.name: Jak and Daxter: The Precursor Legacy
The Legend of Zelda: Skyward Sword
The Legend of Zelda: A Link Between Worlds

f_online_cs.name: Internet Client-Server Play
f_online_cs.summary: Internet client-server play puts one authoritative server in charge of game state while clients predict their own actions locally, keeping play responsive across connections that are slow and unreliable.
prose: Authority sits in one place. Clients send inputs rather than outcomes, the server simulates and returns state, and each client meanwhile predicts the result of its own input so movement feels immediate; when the server disagrees, the client is corrected, which is the rubber-banding players recognise. Interpolation smooths other players' movement, and lag compensation rewinds the world briefly to judge whether a shot connected.

id Software released Quake in 1996, and the network model that made internet play workable arrived through an updated client later that year, written after the original struggled over dial-up connections. Client-side prediction was the crucial addition. Constraints were physical: latency across the public internet cannot be removed, so the engineering problem was never speed but disguising delay convincingly enough to keep matches fair.

Everything social in the medium since rests on this architecture, from persistent worlds to matchmaking to competitive leagues, and an authoritative server remains the main defence against cheating. Costs are ongoing rather than one-off, because servers must be paid for, which turned multiplayer into a service with a lifespan. Games whose servers close become unplayable in a way that cartridges never were.

adoptedBy.name: Age of Empires II: The Age of Kings

f_procgen_loot.name: Procedural Loot Tables
f_procgen_loot.summary: Procedural loot tables assemble items as they drop, combining a base type with randomly rolled modifiers, so two weapons of the same kind can differ enormously in quality and effect.
prose: Each drop is built rather than chosen. A base item is picked from a table weighted by monster type and level, then affixes are rolled onto it: extra damage, resistances, attribute bonuses, each within a numeric range. Rarity tiers determine how many affixes appear, and colour coding signals the tier at a glance. Two items with identical names and artwork can therefore be worthless or run-defining.

Blizzard North built the system into Diablo in 1996, solving a content problem with arithmetic. A hand-authored item list has a fixed size and is exhausted in a single playthrough, while a generator with a few hundred components produces effectively unlimited variants. Randomised treasure was already standard in tabletop role-playing rules and earlier dungeon crawlers; what Diablo added was speed, presentation and an unbroken stream of drops.

Loot became the reason to keep playing, and a genre reorganised itself around drop rates, trading and endgame farming. Consequences reach past design. Variable rewards on a fast cycle hold attention unusually well, a property later attached directly to money, and item value grew legible enough to trade for real currency. Whether the loop is craft or conditioning is argued today in almost identical terms.

f_inventory_grid.name: Spatial Inventory Grid
f_inventory_grid.summary: A spatial inventory grid gives every item a shape and footprint in a fixed rectangle of cells, so carrying capacity becomes a packing problem rather than a list with a weight total.
prose: Space is a grid. A sword occupies three cells, a ring one, a two-handed axe six, and awkward shapes strand gaps that nothing else fits into. Deciding what to keep means comparing value per cell, rearranging, and occasionally abandoning a good item because it will not sit anywhere. Chests, belts and larger bags become upgrades in themselves, since the resource actually being managed is room.

Blizzard North shipped Diablo in 1996 with a grid suited to a game generating far more loot than any player could keep. Constraint gave the drops meaning, because an endless item generator with no limit produces no decisions at all. Capcom's Resident Evil arrived the same year using a slot-limited variant for tension rather than economy, so two unrelated genres reached for the same restriction at almost the same moment.

Friction turned inventory management into gameplay, which players either enjoy as a puzzle or resent as clerical work; whole games are built on each opinion. Time is the direct cost, much of it spent shuffling rectangles instead of playing, and the mechanic scales badly once drop rates climb. Modern loot games often keep the grid as texture while removing its teeth through auto-sorting, stacking and effectively unlimited storage.

f_follow_cam.name: Trailing Follow Camera
f_follow_cam.summary: A trailing follow camera is a viewpoint that chases the player character with its own physics, collision and framing rules, rather than sitting at a fixed distance behind them.
prose: Camera is treated as an object. It has a target position behind and above the character, a spring that pulls it there, collision so it does not enter walls, and logic to swing around obstacles or reframe during a fall. Player usually gets partial manual control on top. Every one of those behaviours changes the meaning of the control stick, because forward is defined relative to wherever the camera ended up.

Nintendo EAD had to solve this for Super Mario 64 in 1996, the first time a large audience moved a character freely through 3D space. Nothing about it was obvious. A camera on a rigid pole clips through geometry, one that snaps instantly is nauseating, and one that always faces the action removes any ability to look ahead. Fiction papered over the machinery by making the camera a character with a name.

Camera work became a permanent discipline. Studios now employ people whose job is framing, and third-person camera failures remain among the most common complaints about otherwise finished games. Solutions since have mostly narrowed the problem rather than settled it, through lock-on, corridors, shoulder cameras or scripted angles. Whether the player or the system should own the view is still argued title by title.

adoptedBy.name: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time

f_true_3d_poly.name: True Polygonal Free-Look Space
f_true_3d_poly.summary: True polygonal free-look space renders a world of arbitrary geometry with a camera free to rotate on every axis, so rooms can sit above rooms and the view can point anywhere.
prose: Levels are built from convex polygonal volumes rather than a grid, and the renderer sorts and clips them using precomputed visibility data so only what can be seen is drawn. Players, projectiles and monsters occupy the same coordinate space with real height, and the camera pitches as well as turns. Aiming becomes a genuinely three-dimensional problem, and architecture can include stairs, bridges, shafts and overlapping floors.

id Software's Quake arrived in 1996, after several years in which the studio's own grid renderers had exhausted what could be faked. Software rendering on fast consumer processors, joined by early 3D accelerator cards, made honest geometry affordable at last. Design followed the technology: since the engine no longer required right angles and uniform heights, the game was built around vertical space, and the mouse became the standard way to look.

Free geometry made place-making possible and pushed the medium toward simulated architecture, physics and cameras that can go anywhere. Costs were real. Art budgets grew, level design got harder to read, motion sickness became a design concern, and the divide between mouse and gamepad starts here. Nearly every 3D control and camera convention of the following decade is an argument about how to make this space usable.

adoptedBy.name: Star Wars Jedi Knight: Dark Forces II

f_crafting.name: Crafting From Gathered Materials
f_crafting.summary: Crafting from gathered materials lets players convert raw inputs collected in the world into finished equipment and goods, giving non-combat activity an economy and the setting a visible supply chain.
prose: Recipes join inputs to outputs. Gathering yields materials with tiers and locations, a recipe consumes set quantities, and skill, tools or a workstation may gate the result or determine its quality. Depth comes from the graph rather than the act: multi-stage chains where intermediate goods feed later ones turn a world's geography into a production problem, and make some regions worth visiting only for their raw materials.

Origin Systems included player crafting in Ultima Online in 1997 because a persistent world needs occupations that are not adventuring. Letting players smith, tailor and build gave the server an internal economy where goods came from labour rather than from monster drops, and it gave thousands of subscribers a role in a world that could not possibly hand every one of them a heroic quest.

Manufacturing supplies purpose for exploration, a sink for loot and a reason for trade, which is why it now appears in almost every genre. Fatigue is the standard complaint, since many implementations require materials nobody chooses to gather and hide upgrades behind counting, so the system becomes an inventory tax. Games that survive that usually make gathering pleasant in itself, or keep recipes rare and consequential.

adoptedBy.name: The Last of Us Part II

f_directional_block.name: Directional Attack and Block
f_directional_block.summary: Directional attack and block give strikes and guards a spatial orientation, so an overhead cut has to be met with a high guard and reading the angle matters as much as reacting to the timing.
prose: Geometry replaces a single block button. Each attack carries a direction, high, low, left or right, and the defender picks a matching stance or guard; a mismatch lets the blow through or trades badly. Stance systems extend the idea by grouping moves under postures with different coverage, so choosing a stance is a standing prediction about what the opponent intends rather than a moment-to-moment reaction to what they do.

Light Weight built Bushido Blade in 1997 around the argument that sword fights end quickly. Discarding health bars in favour of limb damage and lethal strikes made blocking a question of where the blade is rather than how much damage remains, and a directional guard was the only way to express that with a controller. Its immediate ancestors are the fighting game combo systems it was deliberately rejecting.

Melee as reading rather than execution has persisted, mostly in third-person action games that want swordplay to feel like an argument between two people. Adoption stayed narrow because the scheme needs either many buttons or an analogue stick the camera also wants, and because directional guessing frustrates players who cannot see a wind-up clearly. Motion controls and stance systems are two different answers to that same input problem.

adoptedBy.name: The Legend of Zelda: Skyward Sword

f_faction_rep.name: Faction Reputation
f_faction_rep.summary: Faction reputation tracks standing with each group in the world separately, so helping one side costs you with another and the question becomes whose side you are on, not whether you are good.
prose: Every organisation keeps its own ledger. Kills, thefts, completed contracts and dialogue choices move a value attached to that faction, and the value drives concrete world state: guards who attack on sight, merchants who refuse to trade, quests that appear or vanish, safe passage through a district. Many systems propagate standing across alliances and rivalries, so a favour done for one militia automatically damages your position with the group it fights.

Interplay Productions built the system into Fallout in 1997 for a setting with no clear heroes. Its wasteland was full of settlements with incompatible interests, and a single morality score could not express the difference between raiders, a merchant town and a cult. Standing per group also made the world legible without a narrator, because a player can infer a faction's politics from what it rewards and what it punishes.

Splitting morality into constituencies solved the optimisation problem only partly. Players still maximise standing wherever they can, but the choices now trade against each other, and a world state that visibly diverges is harder to fake than a slider. Costs land on content: every faction needs writing, quests and an ending, and testing has to cover players who have made themselves hostile to everyone. Irreversible lockouts remain a common complaint.

f_haptic_feedback.name: Haptic Force Feedback
f_haptic_feedback.summary: Haptic force feedback sends information through the controller as vibration or resistance, giving games a channel that costs no screen space and requires no reading or translation.
prose: Motors, and later voice coils and actuators, are driven by the game with a strength and duration chosen per event. A hit, an engine, a footstep on gravel or a low warning can each have a signature the hands learn. Because the channel is neither visual nor verbal, it works while the player is looking elsewhere, and it carries emotional weight out of all proportion to its bandwidth. Overuse flattens it into noise.

Nintendo EAD shipped Star Fox 64 in 1997 with the Rumble Pak, an accessory that bolted a motor onto the controller, and used it for impacts and damage in a game where the player is constantly under fire. Force feedback existed earlier in arcade cabinets and flight hardware; a cheap console accessory made it ordinary. Within a generation vibration was built into standard controllers and assumed by nearly every game.

Touch turned out to be good at exactly what the screen is bad at: confirming a hit that happened off-frame, communicating surface and weight, and building tension without a sound cue. It also became an accessibility feature, and later a subtle one, as actuators improved enough to suggest texture and resistance. Downsides are cost, battery drain, and a long history of rumble used as generic emphasis.

f_vehicle_sim.name: High-Fidelity Vehicle Physics
f_vehicle_sim.summary: High-fidelity vehicle physics model tyre grip, weight transfer and drivetrain behaviour closely enough that driving becomes a skill of managing load, and tuning a car matters as much as steering it.
prose: Grip is computed, not assigned. A tyre model converts load, slip angle and surface into force, weight shifts between wheels under braking and cornering, and the drivetrain decides which wheels receive torque, so identical inputs produce different results depending on what the car was doing a moment earlier. Setup values such as gearing, downforce and suspension stiffness feed the same equations, which is what makes tuning consequential.

Polyphony Digital shipped Gran Turismo in 1997 on hardware finally able to run that arithmetic per wheel at frame rate, and paired it with licensed production cars and a career built on buying and modifying them. Serious simulation had existed on personal computers for years in specialist titles, so what 1997 established was that a mass console audience would accept a demanding physical model if the surrounding game was about ownership.

Racing became an equipment hobby, complete with tuning forums, driving-line theory and eventually consumer wheels and pedals, while the same physics work later served open-world games where cars are transport rather than sport. Realism cuts against accessibility, so most series ship assists that quietly simplify the model underneath, and the argument about how much simulation a general audience actually wants has never been settled.

f_parry_riposte.name: Parry and Riposte Window
f_parry_riposte.summary: A parry and riposte window rewards deflecting an incoming attack within a few frames, converting a successful defence into a guaranteed counterattack rather than a safe but passive block.
prose: Timing is everything. Pressing the defensive input just before contact triggers a state that negates damage and leaves the attacker exposed for a fixed period, long enough to guarantee a punish. Missing the window normally leaves the defender open instead, which is exactly the point: a parry is a bet that you know what is coming. Systems differ in how wide the window is and whether repeated attempts carry any risk.

Capcom introduced the parry in Street Fighter III: New Generation in 1997, at a moment when the studio wanted to reset a genre it had defined and to reward reading an opponent over drilling strings. Defence had been the dull half of fighting games, and making it an aggressive act with a price restored the guessing game. Earlier titles had counter moves, but the frame-tight window with an assured reply is what survived.

Migration out of fighting games was rapid and close to total. Parrying gives action, stealth and role-playing designers a way to make dangerous enemies fair without lowering their damage, since the player always has an answer that depends on attention rather than statistics. Costs are real: a strong parry can flatten a combat system into one correct verb, and players who cannot hit the timing get locked out of content the design assumes is reachable.

f_mmo_persistent.name: Persistent Shared World
f_mmo_persistent.summary: A persistent shared world runs continuously on servers whether or not any particular player is present, so thousands of people inhabit one economy, one geography and one accumulating history.
prose: State lives on the server and never resets. Characters, houses, items and prices persist between sessions, resources are shared rather than copied per player, and the consequences of other people's actions are waiting when you log in. Scale forces decisions single-player games never face: scarcity has to be managed, harassment has to be policed, and every mechanic is eventually exploited by someone with more time than the designers.

Origin Systems launched Ultima Online in 1997 with a simulated world of resources, crafting and player conflict. Credit here is contested and worth stating plainly: text-based multi-user dungeons had run persistent shared worlds since the late 1970s, and at least one graphical predecessor reached market before 1997. What Ultima Online demonstrated was that the model could work at commercial scale behind a subscription.

Persistence produced the most ambitious social experiments the medium has attempted, along with the discovery that a simulated world full of people behaves less like a story and more like a settlement, complete with theft, cartels and inflation. Costs are severe: servers, moderation and continuous new content, funded by subscriptions that require the world to keep growing, which is why so many closed and took their history with them.

adoptedBy.name: Final Fantasy XIV: A Realm Reborn

f_photo_mode.name: Photo Mode
f_photo_mode.summary: Photo mode hands the player a free camera, a pause button and a set of lens controls, turning a running game into a subject that can be framed, composed and exported.
prose: Simulation is frozen or slowed, the camera detaches from gameplay constraints, and the player gets focal length, aperture, exposure, filters and often character posing. Result is saved as an image the game never rendered during play. Implementation is harder than it looks, because assets built to be seen from one angle at speed must hold up at rest, and hidden geometry becomes suddenly visible.

Polyphony Digital's Gran Turismo in 1997 included replay and photo functions fitting a game whose subject was cars as objects of admiration rather than merely vehicles to drive. Racing games had the necessary parts already, since replays were standard and cars were the most detailed assets in the engine. Later the feature spread because consoles added capture and sharing, which made screenshots a distribution channel.

Player-owned cameras changed how games circulate. Marketing images now come from audiences, virtual photography became a practice with its own criticism, and studios began building environments to reward looking rather than only passing through. Costs are modest but real: art must survive scrutiny, performance budgets must allow a paused free camera, and some games discover their illusions do not withstand a lens that goes anywhere.

adoptedBy.name: The Last of Us Part II

f_guilds.name: Player Guilds and Clans
f_guilds.summary: Player guilds and clans are formal in-game organisations with names, membership rolls and ranks, letting groups of players hold a shared identity and coordinate well beyond a single session.
prose: Membership is recorded by the server. A guild has a roster, officer ranks with permissions, a private chat channel, often a shared bank, and sometimes a tag displayed beside every member's name. Those features convert an informal friend group into an institution with succession problems, resource disputes and a recruitment policy, none of which the game ever wrote a rule about but all of which it now supports.

Origin Systems supported guilds in Ultima Online in 1997 because players in shared worlds form groups regardless, and unsupported groups are invisible to the game. Formalising membership let the server enforce shared property, mark allegiance during open conflict, and give organisations something concrete to fight over. Text-based multi-user worlds had featured player groups for years, so the innovation was tool support rather than the social fact.

Obligation to other people is the most powerful retention mechanism the medium has found, which is both its value and its ethical problem: players log in because friends are counting on them, not always because they want to. Guilds also carry social work the game cannot, supplying teaching, moderation and welcome, and their collapse is usually what ends an individual player's involvement entirely.

adoptedBy.name: Final Fantasy XIV: A Realm Reborn

f_lock_on.name: Contextual Lock-On Targeting
f_lock_on.summary: Contextual lock-on targeting binds the camera and the character to a chosen enemy, keeping both facing each other so that movement becomes circling and attacks land where intended.
prose: Pressing the button asks the game to pick a valid target nearby, usually the nearest thing in view, and to hold the camera behind the player looking at it. Movement input is reinterpreted as strafing and circling around that target, and attacks, blocks and thrown items are aimed automatically. System also does tutorial work, since what a game chooses to lock onto tells the player what currently matters.

Nintendo EAD introduced Z-targeting in Ocarina of Time in 1998, having found that sword combat in a free 3D space was nearly unplayable with the era's cameras. Reference point was reportedly the way two fighters square off, a relationship rather than a set of angles. Solution folded the camera problem and the aiming problem together, which is why it spread so quickly to games with no swords in them.

Legibility came at the price of a certain flattening, because a locked fight is effectively a two-dimensional duel on a circle, and games with many attackers must decide how to switch between them. Whole subgenres accepted the trade and built on it, notably the FromSoftware lineage, where locked duelling is the entire combat model. Games that reject it, keeping free aim in melee, are still treated as making a statement.

origin.name: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time

adoptedBy.name: The Legend of Zelda: Majora's Mask
The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker
The Legend of Zelda: Twilight Princess
The Legend of Zelda: Skyward Sword

f_3d_audio_stealth.name: Diegetic 3D Audio Information
f_3d_audio_stealth.summary: Diegetic three-dimensional audio carries real tactical information, using footstep material, distance, direction and occlusion so that a player can locate and identify threats by listening alone.
prose: Sound is simulated rather than decorated. Footsteps differ by surface, so a guard on stone is audible much further than one on carpet; volume falls with distance, walls muffle and redirect, and positional mixing lets a player place a source behind a door. Guards make noise deliberately, muttering and jangling, while players make it accidentally, so listening and staying quiet are two halves of one skill.

Looking Glass Studios built Thief: The Dark Project in 1998 around a first-person game in which the player mostly avoids what they can hear, and invested in an audio system able to report material, distance and occlusion. Consumer sound hardware had just made positional mixing practical. Necessity shaped it further, because a game played in darkness cannot rely on the eyes to carry threat information.

Ears became a primary sensor, and the technique carried into horror, competitive shooters and survival games, where footstep audio is now a core skill. Equipment and access are the costs. Positional information assumes headphones and unimpaired hearing, so games leaning on it exclude players unless visual indicators are added, which is now common practice. Speaker layouts, streaming compression and mixing choices all degrade the signal further.

f_cinematic_direction.name: Directed In-Engine Camera Language
f_cinematic_direction.summary: Directed in-engine camera language applies film grammar, cuts, dollies and deliberate framing, to a running game engine so that story scenes and playable moments share one continuous world.
prose: Instead of playing a prerendered video, the game scripts its own camera through the live scene: shots are chosen, characters blocked, transitions cut like film, with the same models and lighting used moments earlier. Because nothing is pre-baked, a scene can reflect what the player is wearing, carrying or has already done, and a director can move between cinema and control without a hard boundary.

Konami Computer Entertainment Japan's Metal Gear Solid in 1998 arrived once 3D consoles could hold characters expressive enough to act, and after full-motion video had proved that cutting to filmed footage broke the illusion. Working in-engine kept one visual world intact. Hideo Kojima's team treated shot selection, radio conversations and codec framing as authorial tools, setting expectations for how a cinematically ambitious game should look.

Approach produced the modern narrative blockbuster and, eventually, games that never cut away at all. Debate about it has not resolved, since taking the camera means taking control, and critics have argued since the 1990s that authored framing is borrowed prestige rather than a native strength. Practical costs are large too: a scripted camera constrains level layout, animation budgets balloon, and localisation must handle performance rather than text.

adoptedBy.name: Metal Gear Solid 2: Sons of Liberty
Metal Gear Solid 4: Guns of the Patriots

f_detection_meter.name: Explicit Detection Feedback
f_detection_meter.summary: Explicit detection feedback shows players what enemies currently perceive, using meters, icons, vision cones or sound indicators to turn a hidden system into readable and teachable information.
prose: Perception is drawn on screen. Awareness may appear as a filling meter above a guard, a symbol at the moment of detection, a cone on the map showing where someone can see, or a marker for the last known position they are moving toward. Some games render noise as expanding rings. Whatever the form, the display describes the enemy's belief rather than the truth of the situation.

Konami Computer Entertainment Japan added radar and alert indicators to Metal Gear Solid in 1998 because a three-dimensional stealth game is otherwise played by guesswork. Camera limits made judging sightlines by eye unreliable, and nobody learns a system whose rules they never observe. Exposing the internal state converted a source of frustration into a tactical display, and turned difficulty into a matter of planning rather than luck.

Stealth became teachable, and skill shifted from cautious crawling toward reading and manipulating attention. Immersion pays for it. A cone drawn on a map is a chart rather than a place, and players watching the chart stop watching the world, which is why some games withhold the display or offer a mode without it. Where exactly the line falls between fairness and hand-holding remains unsettled.

adoptedBy.name: Metal Gear Solid 2: Sons of Liberty

f_alert_states.name: Graduated Alert States
f_alert_states.summary: Graduated alert states move enemies through named stages of awareness, from unaware to suspicious, alerted and searching and back again, so being spotted becomes recoverable rather than terminal.
prose: Awareness is a state machine with timers. A noise pushes a guard into suspicion and sends them to investigate; a clear sighting triggers full alert, reinforcements and a countdown. Finding nobody drops the group into a search phase where patrols widen and behaviour stays cautious, and only after that does the level return to normal. Each stage carries its own music, animation set and rules of engagement.

Konami Computer Entertainment Japan built the system for Metal Gear Solid in 1998, when three-dimensional space made perfect avoidance unrealistic and instant failure intolerable. Earlier stealth games often restarted the level on detection, punishing experimentation exactly where it was most needed. Modelling awareness as a curve let designers keep tension alive after a mistake, and gave players something to do with that mistake besides reloading.

Stealth became a genre people finished rather than abandoned, and the vocabulary spread well beyond it into open worlds and horror. Pacing and honesty are what it costs. Waiting out a search timer inside a locker is dull, and the states feel arbitrary when a guard forgets a body or remembers one forever. Designers still argue whether a return to unaware is a mercy or a lie the fiction cannot carry.

adoptedBy.name: Metal Gear Solid 2: Sons of Liberty
Metal Gear Solid 4: Guns of the Patriots
The Last of Us Part II

f_ads.name: Iron-Sight Aim-Down-Sights
f_ads.summary: Aiming down sights is a second firing mode that raises the weapon to eye level, trading movement speed and peripheral vision for accuracy and a clearer sight picture.
prose: Holding a button swaps to a tighter field of view aligned with the weapon's iron sights or optic, narrows or removes spread, slows walking, and usually changes how recoil behaves. Player therefore chooses between mobility and precision several times a second, and the choice is legible to opponents because the animation is visible. Weapon balance is expressed largely through how that transition feels and how long it takes.

Red Storm Entertainment's Rainbow Six in 1998 came out of a simulation tradition that wanted weapon handling to matter, and it is the usual credit for the modern toggle. Precedents exist, since scopes and zoom modes were common well before, so the defensible claim is narrower: making unscoped iron sights a routine whole-weapon mode rather than a sniper's special case. Console shooters later made it the default.

Toggle gave designers a dial for pacing, and it is a large part of why modern shooters feel deliberate where arena shooters feel fast. Costs are aesthetic and competitive. Time spent in sights is time with a restricted view, the mode rewards holding angles over moving, and many games attach aim assist to it, which quietly changes what skill is being tested. Arena purists have rejected it for decades.

adoptedBy.name: Call of Duty: World at War

f_light_shadow.name: Light-and-Shadow Stealth
f_light_shadow.summary: Light-and-shadow stealth measures illumination and sound as concrete quantities, so standing in darkness or moving across soft ground genuinely changes whether guards can perceive the player.
prose: Brightness at the player's position is sampled and reported, often through a visible gem or meter, and guards test against that value rather than against a scripted trigger. Sound behaves the same way: footsteps carry differently on stone, wood, carpet and water, and slowing down quietens them. Water arrows extinguish torches and moss arrows lay quiet ground, so lighting and materials become a system the player edits.

Looking Glass Studios shipped Thief: The Dark Project in 1998, having built a first-person game around avoidance at a moment when the perspective meant shooting. Their engine could report light values and surface materials cheaply, which made those properties usable as rules rather than decoration. Design followed the technology: if darkness can be measured, a level can be composed in light the way another game composes cover.

Lighting stopped being art direction and became level design, a shift visible in every stealth game since and in how immersive sims treat environments as systems. Graphics brought the costs. Modern dynamic lighting makes a stable, readable darkness value hard to guarantee, and players resent being spotted in a shadow that looked solid. Several later games abandoned measured light for scripted visibility simply because it is easier to tune.

f_quest_log.name: Quest Journal
f_quest_log.summary: A quest journal records what characters have told the player, tracking objectives, leads and completion states so several storylines can be followed at once without keeping notes on paper.
prose: Conversations and events write entries into a list openable at any time: who asked, for what, where, and what has been done so far. Entries update as circumstances change and move to a completed section once resolved. Most journals separate central threads from optional ones, and many quote the original dialogue, so the log doubles as a record of who said what and how trustworthy they seemed at the time.

BioWare built one into Baldur's Gate in 1998, when computer role-playing games were opening outward: dozens of concurrent leads, a large map, and no fixed order in which to pursue them. Before that, players kept written notes, a practice carried over from tabletop play and adventure games. Automating it was less a creative leap than an admission that a design with forty open threads cannot rely on anyone's memory.

Nonlinear questing became practical, and the journal grew into the scheduling interface for entire open worlds. Costs are subtle. A log that states objectives plainly discourages listening, since the answer will be written down regardless, and it nudges writers toward instructions rather than conversation. Certain games now offer journals that record only what was said, without directions, precisely to hand attention back to the fiction.

adoptedBy.name: Baldur's Gate II: Shadows of Amn
Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic II - The Sith Lords
Ni no Kuni: Wrath of the White Witch

f_ragdoll.name: Ragdoll Physics
f_ragdoll.summary: Ragdoll physics simulate a body as jointed rigid parts once it loses control, so falls and deaths are computed from momentum and collision rather than played back from a fixed animation.
prose: A skeleton is rebuilt as physics objects. Limbs become rigid bodies joined by constraints that roughly match human range of motion, and when the game hands control to the solver the body falls under gravity, catching on stairs and railings on the way down. Results are unrepeatable by construction, which is both the appeal and the problem: no two deaths look alike, and none can be art-directed in advance.

DreamWorks Interactive shipped Jurassic Park: Trespasser in 1998 with an unusually ambitious full-body simulation, and it was widely judged a failure at the time, its arm controls and unstable bodies becoming a standing joke. Credit is therefore awkward: the technique only became reliable in other studios' hands a few years later. What Trespasser demonstrated, expensively, was that simulated bodies had become computationally possible on consumer machines.

Simulation replaced animation for one narrow case and changed how worlds felt, because a body that interacts with geometry is evidence that the geometry is real. It also introduced a permanent tonal risk, since physics has no sense of occasion: corpses flail, catch on doorframes and slide downhill, and a solemn death becomes slapstick. Most games now blend authored animation with simulation to keep some control over the moment.

f_note_highway.name: Scrolling Note Highway
f_note_highway.summary: A scrolling note highway renders upcoming inputs as objects travelling toward a fixed judgement line, turning a musical part into something a stranger can sight-read within seconds.
prose: Notes approach along lanes at a speed tied to the tempo, and each lane maps to one control. Hitting a note as it reaches the line scores it, sustained notes are held, and chords arrive as simultaneous rows. Because the display shows the future, the interface teaches continuously: a player reads density and spacing well ahead of time and prepares, rather than reacting to a cue at the moment it lands.

Konami introduced the arrangement with GuitarFreaks in 1998 in arcades, where a machine has seconds to explain itself to somebody standing in front of it holding money. Traditional notation is unreadable at that speed by that audience. Mapping pitch to lanes and time to distance removed any need for musical literacy, and the vertical layout also survives being watched over a player's shoulder by a crowd.

Something genuinely universal came out of it, and the same layout now appears across instruments, dance mats, touchscreens and virtual reality. Trade-offs are musical. Lanes flatten harmony into a handful of positions, so the display teaches pattern recognition more than music, and charting is an authored discipline of wildly varying quality. Scroll speed and readability are accessibility issues that many implementations still ignore.

adoptedBy.name: Guitar Hero III: Legends of Rock

f_ability_cooldown.name: Ability Cooldown Economy
f_ability_cooldown.summary: An ability cooldown economy gates powers by time rather than by a resource pool, so each skill returns after a fixed wait and play gets organised around recharging clocks.
prose: Every ability owns a timer. Using it starts a countdown during which the button does nothing, and the real decisions concern sequencing: which skill to spend now, which to hold for a moment that will matter more, how to cover the gap while the strong option recharges. Unlike mana, cooldowns cannot be stockpiled, so power output is capped per minute rather than per expedition.

Verant Interactive leaned on timers in EverQuest in 1999 because a persistent shared world needs rate limits that a single-player game does not. Mana alone lets a well-supplied player unload everything at once, which breaks group encounters and server economies alike, while a clock throttles output regardless of how many potions someone brought. Timed abilities also gave each class a rhythm that other players could learn and depend on.

Scheduling became the shape of combat, which is why cooldowns underpin team games where readable, predictable power is essential; watching an opponent's timers is itself a competitive skill. Costs include rotation play, in which optimal use degenerates into repeating a memorised sequence, and a peculiar fiction where a hero cannot swing the same sword the same way twice within ten seconds for reasons the world never explains.

adoptedBy.name: Ni no Kuni: Wrath of the White Witch

f_raid_content.name: Coordinated Raid Encounters
f_raid_content.summary: Coordinated raid encounters are large scripted fights that require dozens of players to execute assigned roles in sequence, making the group rather than the individual the unit of play.
prose: Encounters are choreography. A boss moves through phases with telegraphed mechanics, each demanding a specific response from a specific role at a specific moment, and one failure can end the attempt for everybody. Success depends on preparation outside the fight: consumables, gear thresholds, assigned duties and voice communication, which makes a raid as much a scheduling and leadership problem as a mechanical one.

Verant Interactive built encounters at that scale into EverQuest in 1999, drawing on the cooldown economy that made class roles legible and on the persistent world that gave large groups a reason to exist. Motivation was retention: a persistent world needs a top end nobody can exhaust alone, and content requiring forty coordinated people takes months of organisation before it is even attempted once.

Raiding produced the closest thing games have to orchestral performance, and the closest thing they have to unpaid middle management. Costs fall on the people who run them, recruiting, scheduling and mediating, and on developers, who spend enormous budgets on content a minority of subscribers will ever see. Later designs answered by scaling difficulty and group size so the choreography reaches more players.

adoptedBy.name: Final Fantasy XIV: A Realm Reborn

f_weather_sys.name: Dynamic Weather
f_weather_sys.summary: Dynamic weather changes conditions in a game world on its own schedule, sometimes driven by a forecast model, so rain, fog and storms arrive without being staged for a particular scene.
prose: State evolves over time. A weather system holds current conditions, transitions between them by probability or from a stored pattern, and pushes results into rendering, audio and gameplay, where rain may cut visibility, wet ground may change traction, and storms may keep certain characters indoors. Systems with mechanical weight also need forecasting or warning, or players experience them as arbitrary punishment rather than as conditions.

Sega AM2 built weather into Shenmue in 1999 using recorded conditions for the region and period the game depicts, so its skies follow something closer to a historical record than a random roll. Ambition of that kind suited a game measured in daily routine rather than in levels, and it depended on the storage that consoles were only then acquiring in the move to optical media.

Unstageable atmosphere is both the point and the difficulty. Weather makes a world feel indifferent to the story, gives repeated locations variety at almost no content cost, and supplies genuine mechanical pressure in survival designs. It also ruins carefully lit scenes, forces artists to make every location work under every condition, and tempts designers into forcing the weather at dramatic moments, which quietly undoes the system.

adoptedBy.name: The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker
The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild

f_recoil_pattern.name: Learnable Recoil Patterns
f_recoil_pattern.summary: Learnable recoil patterns make a weapon's spray deterministic, so a held trigger climbs and drifts the same way every time and players can cancel it with a memorised mouse movement.
prose: Randomness is removed, or nearly. Each successive shot in a burst is displaced by a fixed offset, producing a repeatable path that players learn to draw in the air and then counter by pulling along its inverse. Accuracy penalties for moving and jumping complete the system, because the pattern only holds while standing still, which turns every engagement into a decision about whether to stop moving.

Counter-Strike began in 1999 as a Half-Life modification by Minh Le and Jess Cliffe, and its weapon handling reflected a preference for consistency over realism: a fight decided by a random number generator cannot be studied. Deterministic spray gave the mod a skill that could be practised alone, which suited the competitive scene forming around it, and later official releases preserved the patterns almost as inherited law.

Fixed patterns create an invisible skill curve, unmentioned in tutorials and enormous in effect, which explains part of the steep gradient between new and practised players in competitive shooters. That opacity is also the standard criticism, since a mechanic nobody explains functions as a barrier; studios have since added practice ranges and visible spray previews. Alternatives that randomise more are usually judged less fair rather than more.

f_companion_approval.name: Companion Approval
f_companion_approval.summary: Companion approval gives each party member a private opinion of the player that rises and falls with choices, gating conversations, side quests, romances and sometimes whether they stay at all.
prose: Each recruitable character carries a hidden number. Dialogue choices, quest outcomes and even which companions you bring along nudge it up or down, and crossing a threshold unlocks a personal quest, a confession, a romance, or a departure in the middle of an act. Because the value is usually invisible, players read approval through reaction lines, which turns companions into ongoing puzzles rather than static bundles of statistics and equipment.

BioWare added the system to Baldur's Gate II: Shadows of Amn in 2000 to fix a problem left by its predecessor, whose party was six competent mercenaries with no interior life. Giving each companion opinions, quarrels and a personal storyline made recruitment a choice about company rather than about statistics. It also cost little structurally, since approval is a counter attached to dialogue nodes the studio was already writing.

Approval turned party members into the reason many people replay, and it introduced a durable design problem at the same time. Optimising affection encourages players to answer as they believe a character wants rather than as they mean, and writers have responded by hiding the meter, adding companions who dislike flattery, or letting relationships simply fail. Romance content in particular draws criticism for treating intimacy as a lock with a known key.

origin.name: Baldur's Gate II: Shadows of Amn

adoptedBy.name: Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic
Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic II - The Sith Lords

f_dual_analog.name: Dual-Analog Move + Look
f_dual_analog.summary: Dual-analog control assigns movement to the left stick and camera aim to the right, the scheme that now underlies almost every console action game and first-person shooter.
prose: Left stick supplies a direction and speed in the world, right stick supplies rotation of the view, and the two are read independently, so a player can strafe one way while looking another. Aiming on a stick needs help, which is why acceleration curves, sensitivity settings and later aim assist became standard parts of the scheme. Skill lies in coordinating two thumbs on tasks that a mouse gives to one hand.

Argonaut Games' Alien Resurrection in 2000 is commonly cited as the first console shooter to use the layout, and it was widely criticised at the time for exactly that. Attribution is genuinely contested, since several PlayStation-era games experimented with twin sticks after the DualShock arrived, and the scheme reached canonical form a year later in Halo: Combat Evolved. Popular memory credits Halo rather than the earlier attempt.

Standardisation is the real consequence. Once two sticks became the assumed interface, console shooters could be designed for it, which shaped weapon handling, enemy placement, movement speed and the whole apparatus of aim assist. It also entrenched a competitive gap between controller and mouse that cross-play still struggles with, and it made the layout so familiar that unrelated genres adopt it without asking whether it fits.

f_two_weapon_limit.name: Constrained Weapon Loadout
f_two_weapon_limit.summary: A constrained weapon loadout limits the player to carrying two guns at once, so every pickup is a decision about what to abandon rather than an addition to an ever-growing arsenal.
prose: Capacity is the whole constraint. With two slots, ammunition scarcity becomes meaningful, weapons can be tuned to fill distinct roles without redundancy, and a level designer can predict roughly what the player is holding on entering a room. Grenades and melee usually sit outside the limit so there is always an answer available, and discarded weapons stay on the ground as a visible, retrievable record of the choice.

Bungie adopted the rule for Halo: Combat Evolved in 2001, partly because a gamepad has nowhere to put a nine-entry weapon wheel and partly because the studio wanted its sandbox readable. Two weapons bind to comfortable buttons and swap in a moment, and an encounter can then be built on the assumption that the player carries one long-range and one close-range option, or has already made a mistake.

Limiting the loadout gave console shooters a clarity their inventory-heavy predecessors lacked, and it pushed level design toward supplying the right weapon near the moment it is needed. Losses are equally clear: the walking-armoury fantasy disappears, experimentation carries a cost, and players who enjoy hoarding find the rule stingy. Games have argued the point ever since, some shipping both schemes and letting the audience pick.

f_destructible.name: Destructible Geometry
f_destructible.summary: Destructible geometry lets players remove or collapse parts of a level's structure during play, so walls, floors and cover become consumable terrain rather than the fixed boundaries of a designed space.
prose: Level surfaces become mutable. Explosives and heavy weapons carve holes, remove supports or delete whole sections, and the game recomputes navigation, line of sight and collision to match. Approaches range from fully deformable geometry to pre-authored breakable pieces that swap in damaged versions, and most shipping games use the second, because it is predictable, cheap to compute and far kinder to multiplayer synchronisation.

Volition shipped Red Faction in 2001 with technology that let players tunnel through rock and blow doorways in walls, marketed openly as the reason the game existed. Its appeal was contrarian: a shooter promising to undermine every assumption a level designer makes about where players will be.
