Revenue could be booked earlier, a committed audience could be sized before content existed, and the announced schedule became a marketing asset in itself.

Studios gained a funded runway for post-launch teams, which is a genuine benefit when the alternative is disbanding them the week after release. Trust pays for it. A pass whose contents disappoint or slip produces a specific kind of anger, and several publishers have cancelled or refunded them. Structurally the model also pushes announcements earlier, since what is being sold is a roadmap rather than a thing.

f_mobile_f2p.name: Mobile Free-to-Play
f_mobile_f2p.summary: Mobile free-to-play designs around short, interruptible sessions, using energy timers, level maps and in-app purchases to monetise a phone audience that plays in minutes rather than hours.
prose: Sessions are built to run a few minutes and to end at a decision point. Attempts are rationed by an energy meter that refills in real time, so failing a level costs a life and eventually costs waiting. Purchases sell the removal of that wait, extra moves at the moment of failure, or boosts that resolve a stubborn level. A map screen tracks progress and shows where friends have reached.

King released Candy Crush Saga in 2012 across phones and a social network, refining mechanics that browser and social games had already established, energy systems and viral invitations among them. Hardware and payment infrastructure had just aligned: touchscreens everywhere, app stores holding a stored card, and a general audience that had never bought a game. Free entry was the only way to reach people who would not evaluate a price at all.

By revenue this became the dominant form of the medium, funded largely by a small share of players spending heavily. Measurement drives the design consequences, since every element is instrumented and tuned against retention and conversion, which favours legible loops and steady friction over authorial risk. Regulators have responded to spending by minors and to undisclosed odds, and several jurisdictions now require refunds, limits or disclosure.

f_meta_progression.name: Run-Persistent Meta-Progression
f_meta_progression.summary: Run-persistent meta-progression lets a failed run leave something permanent behind, so a roguelike's deletion of the character no longer deletes the player's sense of forward movement.
prose: Currency earned during a run survives death and is spent between runs on permanent upgrades, unlocks or new options in the generation pool. Each attempt therefore has two outcomes, the run itself and the deposit it makes. Tuning is delicate: too much persistence turns a skill game into a grind where failure is merely slow progress, too little and the structure offers nothing traditional permadeath did not.

Cellar Door Games released Rogue Legacy in 2013, framing persistence as an inherited family line where each dead hero's gold buys castle upgrades for a descendant. Fiction did a lot of work by making loss narratively appropriate rather than a concession. Timing mattered too, since a broad audience was discovering roguelikes through digital storefronts and finding the traditional form's total erasure hard to accept.

Compromise created the roguelite and with it one of the most commercially reliable structures in independent games, because it converts failure into a progress bar without removing risk. Purists argue that it undermines the point, since a player can eventually buy their way past a challenge they never learned to beat. Best implementations answer that by making persistence widen options rather than raise numbers.

f_battle_pass.name: Seasonal Battle Pass
f_battle_pass.summary: A seasonal battle pass sells a fixed progression track for a limited period, releasing known cosmetic rewards as the buyer completes challenges and climbs tiers before the season expires.
prose: Buying the pass unlocks a numbered track, often a hundred tiers deep. Playing earns points toward the next tier, while daily and weekly challenges accelerate the climb. Rewards are listed in advance and visible from the start, and a thinner free track runs in parallel for everyone else. Everything is bound to a season of fixed length, and tiers left unclaimed when the clock runs out are usually forfeited.

Valve introduced the format for Dota 2 in 2013 as a compendium attached to its annual tournament, with purchases also inflating the prize pool. Fortnite Battle Royale is what generalised it into the industry default a few years later, so credit is genuinely split between the invention and the popularisation. Motivation was partly regulatory: known contents avoid the gambling comparison that loot boxes attracted, and a schedule produces forecastable revenue.

Randomness was traded for obligation. Players know exactly what they will receive and exactly what they must do to earn it, which is fairer and also more demanding, since the reward depends on playing enough before a deadline. Designers gained a lever for steering behaviour through missions, which can distort how a game is actually played. Whether the format respects players or rents their time is argued from both directions.

f_soft_body.name: Soft-Body Deformation
f_soft_body.summary: Soft-body deformation simulates a structure as a flexible network of connected nodes, so an object bends, crumples and tears according to force rather than switching to a pre-made damaged model.
prose: Objects are built from nodes and beams. Each node carries mass and position, each beam carries stiffness and a breaking threshold, and the solver resolves forces between them many times per second, so a collision propagates through the structure as deformation instead of a swapped mesh. Damage is continuous and cumulative: a bent chassis stays bent, wheels misalign, and handling degrades in ways nobody authored in advance.

BeamNG GmbH released BeamNG.drive into early access in 2013 with soft-body simulation as the entire product, descending from the ragdoll work of the late 1990s but applied to vehicles rather than corpses. Timing came down to processing budget, since solving thousands of constrained nodes in real time only became feasible on ordinary multi-core desktop hardware, and even then the simulation costs far more than the graphics around it.

Fidelity here buys spectacle and study rather than gameplay, which is why the technique has stayed specialised. Crash behaviour that follows from physics is compelling to watch and genuinely useful to engineering-minded players, but it complicates everything a conventional game wants: predictable difficulty, repeatable encounters, network synchronisation and a performance budget shared with other systems. Racing games mostly still swap damage models instead.

f_live_service.name: Live-Service Seasonal Content
f_live_service.summary: Live-service seasonal content organises a game as a calendar, with story, activities, rewards and economy arriving in scheduled seasons and frequently expiring when the next season begins.
prose: Operation replaces release. Content lands on a published schedule of seasons and events, weekly resets rotate whatever is worth doing, and much of it is time-limited: a store rotation, an activity, or a storyline that closes for good when the season ends. Servers hold authoritative state so the game can be altered underneath players, and the installed client is expected to update constantly.

Bungie built Destiny in 2014 as a shooter with the operating structure of a massively multiplayer game, financed by a publishing deal that assumed years of support rather than a single sale. Persistent worlds had run seasonal events for a decade, and the season pass had already normalised selling a schedule. Combining them made the calendar itself the product, which suits both recurring revenue and a permanent development team.

Games gained lifespans measured in years and communities with a shared weekly rhythm, which genuinely serves players who want somewhere to return to. Costs are unusually visible. Expiring content cannot be preserved or played later, the schedule presses on players and staff alike, and a game that must always feel current drifts toward a treadmill. Several prominent services have closed entirely, taking everything bought inside them.

f_nemesis_system.name: Procedural Nemesis Hierarchy
f_nemesis_system.summary: A procedural nemesis hierarchy generates individual enemy commanders who remember past encounters, gain rank when they beat the player, and refer to that shared history when they meet again.
prose: Characters are assembled from parts. Each commander receives a name, a voice, a face, strengths, fears and a position in a hierarchy, and every encounter writes to their record: scars from a failed kill, promotion after a victory, a grudge that surfaces later in dialogue. Positions in the hierarchy are contested by the generated characters themselves, so the political structure keeps changing whether or not the player intervenes.

Monolith Productions built the system for Middle-earth: Shadow of Mordor in 2014, combining the generated activity of open-world design with the faction standing that role-playing games had used since the 1990s. Its insight was that memory, not writing, produces attachment: a randomly assembled orc becomes a character the moment he survives an encounter and mentions it afterwards, which authored dialogue cannot manufacture.

Personality generated by rules is the strongest case the medium has made against the assumption that character has to be written, and it remains almost unrepeated. Part of the reason is legal, since the publisher holds a patent covering the method, and part is practical, because the technique needs a large cast of expendable enemies, extensive voice work, and a game structured so that the player will lose repeatedly.

f_rhythm_combat.name: Rhythm-Locked Action
f_rhythm_combat.summary: Rhythm-locked action requires every move and attack to land on the beat, fusing a music game's timing discipline with the tactical decisions of a dungeon crawl.
prose: Movement, attacks and item use each cost one beat, and missing the beat costs a turn or a scoring multiplier. Enemies act on their own rhythmic patterns, so a skeleton that moves every second beat is a timing puzzle as much as a threat. Because the music sets the clock, tempo becomes difficulty, and a faster track compresses the time available to decide where to step next.

Brace Yourself Games released Crypt of the NecroDancer in 2015, joining two genres that solve each other's pacing problems. Turn-based roguelikes let players deliberate indefinitely, which drains tension, while rhythm games have relentless pace and nothing to decide. Locking turns to a beat imposes a clock on the first and gives the second something to think about, and procedurally built floors keep those choices fresh across attempts.

Tension of a specific kind results, since planning happens while a metronome runs, and music stops being accompaniment and becomes the rule set. Reach is limited. Demanding rhythm and tactics together excludes people competent at only one, and the difficulty cannot be softened much without breaking the premise, which is why implementations tend to offer a beat-free mode as an accommodation rather than as a variant.

f_asymmetric_mp.name: Asymmetric Multiplayer Roles
f_asymmetric_mp.summary: Asymmetric multiplayer gives opposing sides different rules, abilities, goals and sometimes cameras, so balance is negotiated between two distinct designs rather than mirrored across one shared set.
prose: One player may see the world in first person, move fastest, and win by catching people; several others share a third-person view, cannot fight directly, and win by completing repairs and escaping. Neither side plays the same game. Balance cannot be verified by symmetry, so it is measured statistically, in escape rates and match length, then adjusted through continuous patches to individual characters on both sides.

Behaviour Interactive released Dead by Daylight in 2016, formalising a structure horror fiction had always implied and that several online games were circling in the same period. Cheap streaming was part of why it landed. One hunter and a group of hunted produce readable drama for an audience, and the killer's viewpoint gives a broadcast a villain. Four-against-one also fits the size of an ordinary group of friends.

Roles created audiences that barely overlap, so many players never touch the other side and patch notes read as partisan. Perpetual rebalancing became the product, with licensed characters supplying its commercial engine. New players pay most of the cost, because the two sides demand unrelated skills and neither teaches the other. Whether asymmetric games can be balanced at all, or only kept in motion, is genuinely unsettled.

f_vast_streaming.name: Planetary-Scale Streaming
f_vast_streaming.summary: Planetary-scale streaming keeps one continuous simulation from ground level to orbit to interstellar space, generating and paging terrain on the fly so no transition needs a loading screen.
prose: Terrain is produced by noise functions evaluated on demand rather than stored, so what sits on disk is a set of rules instead of a map. Detail is generated at whatever resolution the current distance requires, and coordinates are handled at multiple scales to avoid arithmetic breaking down far from the origin. Result is a universe that exists only where someone is looking, and that looks identical to everyone who looks.

Hello Games shipped No Man's Sky in 2016 with a very small team and an ambition only procedural generation could satisfy, since no studio can author quintillions of planets by hand. Seamlessness was the pitch: flying from a planet's surface into space without a cut demonstrated that the whole thing was one system. Launch controversy centred less on the technology, which worked, than on what the generated worlds contained.

Scale at that magnitude buys awe and costs meaning, and the tension is the form's central problem. Generated variety is broad and shallow, so games built this way tend to layer hand-authored content, systems or other players on top. Technically the achievement stuck: continuous scale from centimetres to light years is now a solved engineering pattern, used by flight simulators and factory games with entirely different goals.

f_climb_anywhere.name: Climb-Anything Stamina Traversal
f_climb_anywhere.summary: Climb-anything stamina traversal makes nearly every surface in a world scalable and limits ascent only with a draining meter, replacing invisible walls with an economic decision about routes.
prose: Rather than tagging specific climbable geometry, the system treats slope as the test: if a surface is steeper than walking allows, the character grips it and a stamina bar begins to drain. Refilling requires ledges, food or upgrades, and rain makes hands slip. Player weighs distance against the meter constantly, so the question is not whether a mountain can be climbed but whether this attempt has enough left in it.

Nintendo EPD's Breath of the Wild in 2017 set out to make an open world where curiosity is always rewarded, which is incompatible with terrain that refuses to be touched. Universal climbing removed the need to author paths and let the map be designed as landscape rather than as corridors. Stamina supplied the missing tension, turning what would otherwise be a free pass into a resource problem with visible costs.

Handing route-finding back to the player made a very large map feel personal, since two people cross it differently, and it quietly deleted the fence, the ledge marker and the yellow paint. Side effects followed. Climbing trivialises many encounters, level designers lose control of approach angles, and long ascents are dull by construction. Games that copied the meter often kept the tedium without the underlying promise about terrain.

origin.name: The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild

adoptedBy.name: The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom

f_deck_progression.name: Deck-Building Run Progression
f_deck_progression.summary: Deck-building run progression makes the deck itself the character, assembled from cards offered during a single run and then discarded completely when that run comes to an end.
prose: A run opens with a weak starting deck and a branching map. Each fight offers a card as a reward, shops sell more, and relics rewrite rules for the rest of the attempt. Adding cards dilutes the deck, so refusing a reward is a genuine move and card removal is a service worth paying for. Death resets everything except unlocks, which widen future options rather than strengthen the next attempt.

Mega Crit released Slay the Spire into early access in 2017, joining two forms that had matured separately: the tabletop deck-builder, where a deck is constructed during play rather than before it, and the roguelike run with procedural layout and permadeath. Both are built from randomised, self-contained decisions. Merging them swapped the roguelike's item build for a deck, which is legible, tunable and cheap to author.

Imitators arrived by the dozen, and card-based runs became a default structure for small teams because content scales through combination rather than through art. Costs are the familiar ones for randomised design. A run can be lost to a bad offer rather than a bad decision, and the probability reading that experts do fluently is opaque to newcomers. Balance work is effectively endless.

f_extraction_loop.name: Extraction Risk/Reward Loop
f_extraction_loop.summary: Extraction loops let players carry their own equipment into a hostile map where every gain and loss is permanent, and only reaching an exit point banks what the run produced.
prose: Gear comes out of a persistent stash and goes into a raid. Anything looted from the map, from bodies or from other players joins it, but none of it counts until the player reaches an extraction point and leaves. Death forfeits the loadout to whoever caused it. Timers, limited exits and rival squads on the same map turn every decision to stay a little longer into a wager against rising risk.

Battlestate Games put Escape from Tarkov into paid early access in 2017, reacting against a decade of shooters where dying cost nothing but a respawn timer. Ideas came from survival server culture, where players had improvised the same tension without support, and from roguelike permadeath. Making loss material required a persistent inventory outside the match, so the design leans on an economy layer most shooters have no reason to build.

Stakes returned, and with them a kind of caution competitive shooters had engineered away; players negotiate, flee and hoard. Costs are steep. Losing an hour of accumulation to an unseen shot drives people off quickly, veterans meet newcomers with compounding equipment advantages, and cheating becomes far more lucrative when the loot is real. Studios have argued for years about how much of the punishment is actually load-bearing.

f_battle_royale.name: Shrinking-Circle Battle Royale
f_battle_royale.summary: Shrinking-circle battle royale drops many players into one map without equipment and forces them together using a boundary that contracts on a timer until a single survivor remains.
prose: Around a hundred players enter a large map carrying nothing. Weapons, armour and healing lie scattered as ground loot, so the opening minutes are a scramble that decides how the next twenty go. A playable zone marked on the map shrinks in timed steps, and standing outside it drains health. Death ends the match for that player. Late rounds compress dozens of survivors into a field the size of a village square.

Attribution here is genuinely contested. PUBG: Battlegrounds launched in 2017 and set the commercial template, but its designer had already built battle royale modes as mods for military simulation games and had consulted on an earlier standalone attempt, while Minecraft servers ran last-player-standing events for years before that. Name and premise come from a Japanese novel and its film adaptation. What 2017 added was polish, scale, and a streaming audience ready for it.

Geometry solved a pacing problem deathmatch never answered: without a closing boundary, hiding is optimal and matches do not end. Consequences run both ways. Sessions became long and unrepeatable, so a bad landing costs half an hour, and skill shares the outcome with luck of the draw. Nearly every large shooter added a mode within three years, which flattened the variety of what those games had otherwise been.

f_chemistry_engine.name: Systemic Elemental Chemistry
f_chemistry_engine.summary: Systemic elemental chemistry defines global rules for how fire, water, wind, metal and electricity interact, so any combination of materials behaves the same way wherever the player finds it.
prose: Objects carry material properties and the engine resolves contact between them. Wood burns, fire climbs slopes and follows wind, metal conducts current and attracts lightning during storms, water conducts and extinguishes, and heat rises to lift anything light enough to catch it. Rules are few and universal, so puzzles have solutions the designers never enumerated, and hazards apply to the player exactly as they apply to enemies.

Nintendo EPD built the model into The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild in 2017, drawing on a decade of physics-driven design and on the propagation systems that had appeared in open-world shooters. Its purpose was navigational as much as combative: in a game whose central promise is that any hill can be climbed, players need rules they can reason about rather than a list of permitted interactions.

Consistency is what makes a large world worth experimenting in, and this approach produced the strongest recent argument that systemic design beats authored puzzle content. Costs are considerable. Every new object must be given properties that behave sensibly against all the others, testing becomes combinatorial, and set-piece design gets harder because players will solve a scene in ways the scene was never built to survive.

origin.name: The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild

adoptedBy.name: The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom

f_crossplay.name: Cross-Platform Play
f_crossplay.summary: Cross-platform play allows people on consoles, computers and phones to share matches and friend lists, breaking the convention that each platform maintains a separate, walled player population.
prose: Matchmaking pools merge across hardware, so a console player and a phone player can queue together and see each other on a friends list. Making that work needs one account system layered above the platform accounts, a single networking build, and rules for the input gap, usually by grouping controller users together or by tuning aim assist. Purchases and progression follow the account rather than the device.

Barriers were commercial rather than technical. Platform holders treated their installed base as a moat, and certification practice long discouraged mixing. Epic Games pushed Fortnite Battle Royale onto every device it could reach in 2018 and made exclusion visible to players, who complained loudly to whichever platform was blocking them. Policy shifted within months. Earlier cross-platform experiments existed, but this is the case that changed the defaults.

Lifespan is where the effect shows. A merged pool keeps queue times short, which keeps smaller and older games playable long past the point at which a fragmented population would have collapsed. Competitive costs are real, since mouse aim and controller aim assist do not balance cleanly, and many games now let players opt out of mixed input, quietly rebuilding the walls the feature was meant to remove.

f_ecology_sim.name: Simulated Ecology
f_ecology_sim.summary: Simulated ecology gives animals and townspeople territory, routine and memory, so wildlife hunts, migrates and avoids danger, and a settlement reacts to what the player did there yesterday.
prose: Creatures are agents with needs. Each has a home range, a feeding pattern, predators and prey, and reactions tied to scent, noise and line of sight, so a herd disperses when wolves arrive and carrion draws scavengers without anyone scripting the sequence. Human inhabitants receive the same treatment at smaller scale, remembering recent encounters and responding to the player's clothing, cleanliness and local reputation.

Rockstar Studios shipped Red Dead Redemption 2 in 2018 with simulation at that density because its subject is a landscape more than a plot, and because budget and hardware permitted spending processing on things most players will never see. Modelling animals whose behaviour a given player may witness once, if ever, is a wager that the aggregate impression of a working ecosystem repays the cost.

Detail of this kind rewards slow attention and frustrates players who want a clean route to the next mission, which is the standard complaint against it. Cost is the deeper issue: simulation at this level is available to a handful of studios, and it does not obviously produce a better game, only a more convincing place. Whether that trade is worth making remains genuinely contested.

f_gear_swap_combat.name: Deflect-Focused Posture Combat
f_gear_swap_combat.summary: Deflect-focused posture combat replaces dodging with well-timed deflection, filling an opponent's posture bar until their guard breaks, so duels are won by holding rhythm rather than by managing distance.
prose: Victory runs through the posture bar, not the health bar. Blocking adds posture damage, deflecting adds far more and costs the defender almost nothing, and a broken guard opens a lethal blow regardless of remaining health. Retreating lets an opponent recover, which inverts the usual advice; safe play means staying in range and meeting attacks on the beat, with unblockable moves forcing a different answer at intervals.

FromSoftware built Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice in 2019 from two of its own inheritances, the parry window fighting games had refined since the late 1990s and the stagger bar the studio introduced a decade earlier. Removing character builds and equipment scaling made the change workable: with no statistics to hide behind, timing becomes the only variable, and difficulty can be tuned entirely through enemy rhythm and recovery.

Combat moved closer to a rhythm game than a spacing game, which produced both the design's admirers and its detractors. Players who internalise the beat describe the most legible melee system in the genre; players who cannot find it have no alternative route, because there is nothing to overlevel. That absence of a fallback is the honest cost of taking statistics out of a difficulty curve entirely.

f_ping_system.name: Non-Verbal Ping Communication
f_ping_system.summary: Non-verbal ping communication turns one context-sensitive button into a grammar for marking loot, enemies, places and intentions, letting strangers coordinate closely without speaking or typing.
prose: One button, aimed at something, produces the right message about it: a weapon name with its rarity, an enemy with a direction, a destination, or a warning. Pressing twice escalates to an alert. Each ping appears in the world for teammates, is spoken aloud by the player's character in the listener's language, and is written in the feed. A radial menu covers intentions that pointing alone cannot express.

Respawn Entertainment built the system for Apex Legends in 2019 around an unglamorous observation about squad games. Voice chat carries most coordination, and a large share of players will never use it, whether from shyness, harassment, a shared room or a language mismatch. Rather than treat that silence as a lost cause, the team catalogued the twenty or so things squadmates actually say and gave each one a button press and a spoken line.

Accessibility, localisation and moderation all improved at once, since a ping cannot be abusive and needs no translation. Squads of strangers started playing like squads. Limits are real: pings compress intent into nouns, and complicated plans still need voice. Some designers argue the system also trained players out of talking, replacing a social space with a signalling protocol, though few would give up the coverage it bought.

f_accessibility_suite.name: Comprehensive Accessibility Suite
f_accessibility_suite.summary: Comprehensive accessibility suites bundle dozens of independent options, from full remapping and audio navigation cues to high contrast and tunable aim support, letting players reshape a game around a specific impairment.
prose: Options are separated rather than folded into difficulty. Text and interface elements enlarge, enemies and items can be outlined in flat colour, traversal directions are announced by audio pings, combat can be slowed, timed inputs skipped, and every control remapped including on-screen prompts. Presets exist for blindness, low vision, motor and hearing needs, but each toggle stands alone, so a player composes a configuration instead of picking a tier.

Naughty Dog shipped the suite with The Last of Us Part II in 2020, after years of advocacy from disabled players and after smaller option sets in earlier games had shown what was possible. Scale rather than novelty was the change: roughly sixty settings, tested with the people who needed them, treated as a shipping requirement instead of a patch to be added once reviews were in.

Reach widened and expectations moved with it, so large releases now face questions about their options list at announcement. Production absorbs the cost, because every toggle multiplies the test matrix and some, such as spoken navigation, mean rebuilding systems rather than adding a switch. Debate continues over where access ends and difficulty begins, particularly for games whose authors treat a specific kind of struggle as the point.

origin.name: The Last of Us Part II

f_vr_presence.name: Room-Scale VR Presence
f_vr_presence.summary: Room-scale VR presence tracks a player's head and hands in physical space, making the camera an extension of the neck and the hands into direct manipulators of the world.
prose: Headset and controllers are tracked in six degrees of freedom, so leaning, crouching and reaching become inputs the game cannot ignore. Objects have to be grabbable from any angle, held at any orientation, and thrown with real arm velocity. Because a player can put their face anywhere, no geometry can be a facade, and every convention built on a controlled camera needs rebuilding from scratch.

Valve released Half-Life: Alyx in 2020, several years into consumer VR, as a full-length game rather than a demonstration. Prior attempts had exposed the specific unsolved problems: locomotion that does not induce sickness, hands that interact without a button for every verb, and pacing for a medium where players stop to examine shelves. Answers were mostly conservative, including teleport movement options and heavy signposting of interactable objects.

Presence changes what identical content means, since scale, threat and intimacy all read differently once the body is involved. It also imposes hard limits: sessions are short, comfort constrains movement, hardware audiences are small, and no amount of fidelity fixes the fact that a player's living room has walls. Whether this becomes a platform or stays a specialised mode is unresolved, and the economics remain unproven.
